Hexadecimal and byte streams

An encoding of bytes, not by itself an encryption method.

Two digits per byte
Hexadecimal uses 0–9 and a–f for values 0–15. Each digit encodes four bits; two encode one byte. Hex 41 is decimal 65, the ASCII byte for A. Leading zeros matter.

Read one pair by place value

For a two-digit hexadecimal byte, multiply the left digit’s value by 16 and add the right digit’s value. The letters a, b, c, d, e and f stand for 10, 11, 12, 13, 14 and 15. Uppercase and lowercase denote the same values.

	Hex pair	Calculation	Decimal value	Eight bits

	04	0 × 16 + 4	4	0000 0100

	41	4 × 16 + 1	65	0100 0001

	5d	5 × 16 + 13	93	0101 1101

	77	7 × 16 + 7	119	0111 0111

	ff	15 × 16 + 15	255	1111 1111


The space in each bit string separates the two four-bit groups for readability. A byte has eight bits and can hold an unsigned value from 0 through 255. Interpreting that byte as a character is another step: 65 represents A in ASCII, but arbitrary payload bytes need not form readable text.

Leading zeros preserve byte boundaries

As integers, hexadecimal 4 and 04 have the same value. As a written byte stream, each byte still needs two digits. For example, 04 10 encodes two bytes with decimal values 4 and 16. Removing the first zero leaves 410, which has an unmatched digit; it does not encode the same two-byte stream under this convention.

The 0x prefix marks an integer literal in Python, as in 0x41 == 65. It is not part of the payload’s hexadecimal digit pairs. Python’s bytes.fromhex("41") decodes a byte, while bytes.fromhex("0x41") rejects the prefix. Likewise, do not convert an entire payload to an integer and back without preserving its byte length: leading zero bytes can otherwise disappear.

Written characters versus decoded bytes

A byte written 04 is one byte whose value is four. It is not the two text characters “0” and “4.” In the LP1-00 body, the first six hexadecimal characters are 775d04; decoding them gives three bytes, 77 5d 04. Encoding the literal characters as ASCII instead would give six bytes, 37 37 35 64 30 34.

hex_text = "775d04"
decoded = bytes.fromhex(hex_text)
characters = hex_text.encode("ascii")
print(decoded.hex(" "))    # 77 5d 04
print(characters.hex(" ")) # 37 37 35 64 30 34
assert len(decoded) == 3
assert len(characters) == 6

This is why the XOR trace operates after hex decoding. The characters used to write a byte and the byte they represent are different inputs.

Decode a cover body
from pathlib import Path
body = Path("exports/steganography/lp1-00.body.txt").read_text()
data = bytes.fromhex(body)
assert len(data) == 991
Whitespace may separate complete byte pairs. Each of the first three bodies has 1,982 hex digits and decodes to 991 bytes. Those bytes need not be readable. The next step is bytewise XOR.

Run from the extracted reference-data bundle or the repository root. Python’s bytes.fromhex accepts whitespace between complete byte pairs and either letter case. An unmatched final digit or a non-hex character raises ValueError. Do not repair such an error by silently dropping characters: check that you selected the message body, kept its bytes intact, and excluded prose or signature delimiters.

Do not decode prose as hex
LP1-03 contains prose followed by hex-encoded JPEG data. Isolate the hex portion before decoding and retain the complete signed body separately from the derivative image.

Exclusive OR (XOR)

The bitwise operation used to combine the three cover-chain payloads.

Exclusive OR, usually written XOR or ⊕, compares bits. Two equal bits give 0; two different bits give 1. Programming languages commonly use ^ for this operation on integers.

A byte example
00001111   (hex 0f)
00110011   (hex 33)
--------
00111100   (hex 3c)
XOR is not addition with carries and is not alphabet arithmetic modulo 29. It works independently at each bit position.

The three-image chain
The signed bodies from LP1-00, LP1-01, and LP1-02 are first decoded from hexadecimal. XOR their corresponding bytes to reconstruct a signed message. XORing their ASCII hex characters would be a different operation.

Follow the first five bytes

Three inputs: count the ones at each bit position

For two bits, XOR means “one or the other, but not both.” When repeated across three inputs, the rule is odd parity: the result is 1 if the number of input ones at that position is odd. It does not mean “exactly one of these three.”

	Number of ones	Example input bits	XOR result

	0	0, 0, 0	0

	1	1, 0, 0	1

	2	1, 1, 0	0

	3	1, 1, 1	1


For the last row, evaluate (1 ^ 1) ^ 1 = 0 ^ 1 = 1. The order of the three inputs does not matter. Apply the same rule independently to each of the eight positions in a byte.

Here is the cover chain’s first byte written in binary. Align the columns; do not add carries between them:

LP1-00   01110111   77
LP1-01   00010111   17
LP1-02   01001101   4d
         --------
XOR      00101101   2d

The rightmost column contains three ones, so its output is 1. The next column contains two ones, so its output is 0. Continue leftward to obtain 00101101. This is the byte value 45 in decimal, written 2d in hexadecimal and interpreted as a hyphen in ASCII. The input and output columns above are bytes, not rune indices or prime sums.

Compare the first five positions

Each row below combines the bytes at one offset in the three decoded streams. Offsets start at zero; all byte values in the table are hexadecimal.

	Offset	LP1-00	LP1-01	LP1-02	XOR output

	0	77	17	4d	2d

	1	5d	a1	d1	2d

	2	04	e1	c8	2d

	3	81	03	af	2d

	4	11	93	af	2d


For offset 0, 0x77 ^ 0x17 = 0x60, then 0x60 ^ 0x4d = 0x2d. The output byte 2d is the ASCII hyphen. The first five output bytes therefore form the five hyphens beginning the signed-message header. That recognizable prefix is a useful checkpoint, but it does not verify the remaining bytes or the signature.

How to replicate

Extract the reference-data bundle and run this Python 3 example from its top-level folder. It reads the three preserved message bodies, decodes them, and prints the reconstructed first line. It does not modify the inputs or write an output file.

from pathlib import Path

pages = ("lp1-00", "lp1-01", "lp1-02")
streams = [
    bytes.fromhex(Path(f"exports/steganography/{page}.body.txt").read_text(encoding="ascii"))
    for page in pages
]
a, b, c = streams
if not (len(a) == len(b) == len(c) == 991):
    raise ValueError("Expected three byte streams of length 991")
combined = bytes(x ^ y ^ z for x, y, z in zip(a, b, c))
print(combined.splitlines()[0].decode("ascii"))
assert combined.startswith(b"-----BEGIN PGP SIGNED MESSAGE-----")
# -----BEGIN PGP SIGNED MESSAGE-----

The length check prevents silent truncation by zip. Do not pad, cycle, or trim these documented inputs. This short example checks length and prefix only. For the full recorded input and output hash checks, run python scripts/reproduce_cover_chain.py. Follow the complete recipe for the separate signature verification and transposition.

Useful identities and their limits
A ⊕ A = 0 and A ⊕ 0 = A. Applying the same XOR mask twice recovers the input. The three inputs can be combined in any order because XOR is associative and commutative. Those identities explain the computation; they do not establish why a particular set of manuscript files should be combined.

The cover payload chain

The cover, warning, and chapter title combine into a signed message and a transposition.

Looking for the cover with compasses? See the illustrated cover and its Blake artwork. It is separate from the title pages discussed here.


Three inputs
LP1-00, Liber Primus, LP1-01, the warning, and LP1-02, Chapter 1 — Intus carry OutGuess payloads. Extract and verify them. Their 1,982-digit bodies decode to three 991-byte streams.

Visible headings and the two title pages.
[Image: LP1-00: title]
LP1-00: title
[Image: LP1-01: warning]
LP1-01: warning
[Image: LP1-02: chapter title]
LP1-02: chapter title
What each stage produces
	Stage	Output to check
	Extract and verify the three messages	One signed hexadecimal body from each of LP1-00, LP1-01, and LP1-02
	Decode hexadecimal	Three separate streams of 991 bytes each
	XOR equal positions	A reconstructed 991-byte signed message
	Take its ciphertext and reorder columns	70 characters, retaining the literal ending ONIO
The visible Welcome text and its Vigenère key are not inputs to this chain. Likewise, the small image embedded in LP1-03 belongs to a different payload. Use exact page IDs when collecting the three source files.
XOR corresponding bytes
What XOR means, with a worked byte example.
XOR produces a 0 bit when input bits agree and 1 when they differ. Compute result[i] = A[i] XOR B[i] XOR C[i] on decoded bytes, not on hexadecimal text characters. For example, 0x0f XOR 0x33 = 0x3c.
python scripts/reproduce_cover_chain.py
python scripts/reproduce_cover_chain.py --output combined.asc
The script checks input and output hashes and refuses to overwrite files. Its 991-byte result is another signed message, requiring its own signature check.

Follow the first byte
The first decoded bytes are 77, 17, and 4d in hexadecimal. Pairing the same position in each stream gives:
0x77 XOR 0x17 = 0x60
0x60 XOR 0x4d = 0x2d
0x2d is the ASCII hyphen, the first character of the reconstructed PGP header. This checks one position only; the script checks the SHA-256 hash of the complete reconstruction. Decode the hex pairs first: XORing the character codes for the printed digits would use different inputs.
All three streams must have equal lengths. Do not pad a short stream, cycle it, or quietly discard unmatched bytes. If lengths disagree, check the extracted bodies and their hashes before proceeding.
Read the columns
Remove spaces from the first two ciphertext lines and arrange the 70 characters in five rows of fourteen:
IDGTKUMLOOARWO
ERTHISUTETLHUT
IATSLLOUIMNITE
LNJ7TFYVOIUAUS
NOCO5JI4MEODZZ
Within each row, take columns in zero-based order 2, 8, 9, 1, 12, 13, 11, 4, 5, 7, 3, 0, 6, 10. Concatenate the five reordered rows from top to bottom. This transposition gives:
GOODWORKULTIMATETRUTHISTHEULTIMATEILLUSIONJOINUSATFV7LYUCMEOZZD5J4ONIO

Follow the first four column selections
The first source row is IDGTKUMLOOARWO. Columns begin at zero, so column 0 contains I, column 1 contains D, and column 2 contains G. Apply the supplied order to that row:
	Output position	Source column	Character
	1	2	G
	2	8	O
	3	9	O
	4	1	D
The first four selected characters spell GOOD. Continue with the remaining ten column indices, then apply the same complete order to each of the next four rows. Here, output positions in the table count from one for readability, while source columns use the zero-based convention required by the script.
The instruction “read the columns” can otherwise be ambiguous: this recipe reorders characters within each row, then joins the rows. It does not read one entire vertical column from top to bottom before moving to the next.
Preserve the literal ending
The exact output ends in ONIO. The historical walkthrough restores a final N to render fv7lyucmeozzd5j4.onion. That character is an interpretation, not a permutation output. This is a historical address, not a claim of current reachability.
The supplied permutation reproduces the known result. It does not show that a unique ordering can be inferred without clues or applied to another page.

PGP signatures and the Cicada key

Verify archived messages and state what verification establishes.

Signature validity and identity
A valid signature ties a signed message to a key. It does not decrypt its body, sign every byte of the enclosing JPEG, or by itself identify a real-world author. Historical association with Cicada is a separate provenance claim.
The full primary fingerprint of the exported key is 6D854CD7933322A601C3286D181F01E57A35090F. Check the key itself, not its filename or short ID.

Verify in a separate keyring
Install GnuPG, create an empty directory named verify-keyring, and run from the repository root:
gpg --no-options --homedir verify-keyring --import exports/steganography/cicada-public-key.asc
gpg --no-options --homedir verify-keyring --fingerprint
gpg --no-options --homedir verify-keyring --verify exports/steganography/lp1-00.signed.asc
gpg --no-options --homedir verify-keyring --verify exports/steganography/cover-chain.signed.asc
Compare the full fingerprint. A good signature and unknown trust can coexist: validity differs from identity-trust assignments. No private key is required.

Read the verification output
For an inspectable status stream, add --status-fd 1:
gpg --no-options --homedir verify-keyring --status-fd 1 --verify exports/steganography/lp1-00.signed.asc
The fresh isolated check produced these status types: GOODSIG, VALIDSIG and TRUST_UNDEFINED. The VALIDSIG line identified the full fingerprint above. The trust warning did not mean the signature failed: this new keyring contained no identity-trust assignments. Do not assign trust merely to silence that warning. GnuPG documents these machine-readable records in its status-format specification.
The displayed user ID, Cicada 3301 (845145127), is a label associated with the key; matching that text is not the same as matching the fingerprint. Keep the verification result, key provenance, and real-world identity claim separate.
If verification fails
No public key: confirm that you imported the shipped key into the same directory supplied to --homedir.
No signed data: check that you selected the preserved .signed.asc block, not the extracted body or decoded binary stream.
Bad signature: compare the file checksum with the manifest and obtain an unchanged copy before drawing conclusions.
Rejected digest: inspect the exact diagnostic and the compatibility note below; a policy rejection differs from a verified signature.
Legacy digest compatibility
Some versions reject historical SHA-1 signatures by policy. If that is the reported cause, repeat this isolated check with --allow-weak-digest-algos on that command only. Record the flag; do not change global settings or treat SHA-1 as suitable for new signatures.

The earlier extraction manifest records the compatibility mode used in that run. A fresh isolated check with GnuPG 2.5.21 on Windows, --no-options, and no compatibility override verified all eight extracted signed blocks plus the reconstructed cover-chain message. The nine-file verification record stores input hashes, status lines, options and version. Do not assume a flag is necessary simply because another verification run used it.
--homedir selects the separate keyring directory; --no-options avoids reading the default options file. See GnuPG configuration options and digest compatibility options.
Why a valid signature is not a whole-file checksum

The preserved messages use a cleartext signed-message wrapper: readable text appears before an armored signature block. Its verification rules normalize the signed text. OpenPGP’s Cleartext Signature Framework specifies canonical CRLF line endings and excludes trailing spaces and tabs on each line from the signature calculation. The separator newline immediately before the signature block is also excluded.

As a result, two files can have different raw-byte SHA-256 checksums while representing the same text for cleartext-signature verification. This is not permission to edit the archive: preserve the original and use the catalogue checksum when the question is whether you have those exact bytes.

Why some lines begin with an extra dash and space

A body line beginning with a hyphen is prefixed with -  in the cleartext wrapper, so it cannot be confused with a wrapper delimiter. For example, the body text -example appears as - -example. Verification uses the unescaped text. This rule is called dash escaping; it is not an extra cipher layer.

Leave the preserved .signed.asc file intact and let GnuPG parse it. If you extract a body for another operation, retain that derivative separately and document the extraction rule.

	Question	Check to use

	Do I have the exact archived signed-block file?	Compare its size and SHA-256 with that file’s catalogue entry.

	Does the cleartext signature verify against this key?	Use GnuPG on the complete signed block and inspect the fingerprint and result.

	Did I decode the extracted hexadecimal body correctly?	Check the derivative’s declared bytes, length and hash under the chain recipe.


These checks complement each other. The cleartext rules above do not mean that arbitrary edits, different words or changed payload digits preserve a signature. They also do not describe every possible OpenPGP signature format.

Different files, different purposes
The manifest separately hashes full extractions, signed blocks, and bodies. Verifying an edited body is not equivalent to verifying the preserved signed block. See extraction and checksums.

---

File hashes and checksums

Identify exact bytes without confusing integrity, signatures, and decryption.

What a checksum establishes
SHA-256 maps bytes to a 256-bit digest, displayed as 64 hex digits. A matching digest identifies expected bytes under the hash’s security assumptions, not their creator. Changed line endings can change a text file’s hash.

Choose the exact file you mean to check

The original JPEG, its thumbnail, a screenshot of the reader, and an image re-saved by an editor can all show the same page while having different bytes. For image analysis or OutGuess extraction, start with the original file linked by the page record. A screenshot is not a replacement for it.

	File you have	Compare against

	An original manuscript JPEG	That image’s entry in the catalogue

	A downloaded ZIP	The ZIP’s own checksum; after extraction, each member has its own checksum

	An extracted signed message	The signed-block entry, not the enclosing JPEG or message-body entry

	A text transcription	The same archived, corrected, or reading version—not a different text layer


Renaming a file does not change its content hash. Resaving it, changing text encoding, or converting LF line endings to CRLF can. File size is a useful preliminary check, but equal sizes alone do not establish equal contents.

Verify directly in the browser

Open Downloads and locate “Verify a downloaded file.”
Select the file you actually saved. The verifier computes SHA-256 locally in the browser and compares its hash and byte count against the catalogue.
Read the returned path, not just the word “Verified.” It identifies the catalogue entry whose bytes matched.

The file is not uploaded by this verifier. A “No exact match” result means no matching entry was found in this catalogue. It does not by itself say that the file is malicious or that an alternative archive is false. Check the intended version, whether the download finished, and whether an application modified the file.

Check a download
# PowerShell
Get-FileHash images/lp1-00.jpg -Algorithm SHA256
# Linux
sha256sum images/lp1-00.jpg
# macOS
shasum -a 256 images/lp1-00.jpg
Compare with the catalog or download entry. Hash the actual file, not its displayed preview.

Run from a folder containing images/lp1-00.jpg, or replace the path with your actual download location. The preserved LP1-00 original is 168,876 bytes and its expected SHA-256 is:

184e6f9de8695d99435c2bef4fd7e304a8a0f704dbe04439fa8bf13c4da395a7

Hexadecimal letter case does not change the digest value; PowerShell may display uppercase. Compare all 64 digits. A leading or trailing excerpt of the digest is not the full check.

Check the files inside an extracted bundle

The reference-data bundle includes a Python 3 checker. From the folder where you extracted it, run:

python scripts/verify_bundle.py REFERENCE-DATA-CONTENTS.json

It checks the recorded size and SHA-256 of each listed file, reports missing or changed members, and leaves your files untouched. A mismatch produces a nonzero exit status. Extra files, such as your own experiment outputs, are not part of this check.

If you extract the original-image bundle into the same folder, its separately named manifest remains available too:

python scripts/verify_bundle.py ORIGINAL-IMAGES-CONTENTS.json

Each bundle has its own named manifest; the transcription bundle uses TRANSCRIPTIONS-AND-READINGS-CONTENTS.json. The older name CONTENTS.json is also included for compatibility, but extracting another bundle into the folder can replace that generic copy. Use the separately named files when combining bundles.

The checker confirms agreement with the manifest you supplied. It does not authenticate that manifest, validate the transcription, or check files omitted from the list. Verify the downloaded ZIP against the published catalog separately when you need to establish which bundle you received.

Why invisible text changes matter

The byte sequence 41 0a is A followed by LF. 41 0d 0a is A followed by CRLF. An editor may display them as the same line, but their hashes differ. This small Python 3 example makes the distinction visible:

from hashlib import sha256

lf = b"A\n"
crlf = b"A\r\n"
print(lf.hex(" "), len(lf))
print(crlf.hex(" "), len(crlf))
assert lf != crlf
assert sha256(lf).digest() != sha256(crlf).digest()
# 41 0a 2
# 41 0d 0a 3

Keep the original byte file and any normalized text as separate artifacts. When documenting an experiment, name the version used and record its checksum before applying transformations. See reproducibility.

A hash check and a signature check answer different questions

A catalogue match checks whether your file agrees with the recorded bytes. Its value depends on which catalogue or source you chose to trust: replacing a file and its expected checksum together would still produce a match. A signature check instead verifies the signed content against a public key, whose provenance must also be established. Neither check proves that an interpretation or proposed cipher solution is correct.

Cleartext PGP verification normalizes certain formatting, including line endings. A valid signature can therefore coexist with a different whole-file hash. See the signed-text rules and dash escaping before comparing these two kinds of result.

LP2-56: exact target, algorithm assumptions, and input bytes.
The puzzle’s hash target
LP2-56 refers to a page identified by a hash. SHA-512 has 128 hexadecimal digits; it differs from this wiki’s SHA-256 distribution checksums. A hash is not normally reversible into its input. Candidate checks need the correct bytes and serialization.
See signatures for signed evidence and prime-minus-one for reproducing the text containing the target.
Sources and verification
Pinned historical walkthrough. Recipes reproduce published controls; they are not new solutions. Local computational verification: 19 October 2026.

Prime values and prime indices

Distinguish a prime from its ordinal, and reproduce the 3299 and 9467 calculations.

A prime’s value and its position in the ordered list of primes are different numbers. Specify which operation you mean before combining a prime with a page number or rune value.

Value versus ordinal
Write p_(n) for the nth prime, using one-based indexing: p_(1) = 2, p_(2) = 3, p_(3) = 5. Looking up p_(3299) gives 30,557. This means that 30,557 is the 3,299th prime; it does not mean that 3,299 has ordinal 30,557.
The rune alphabet instead uses zero-based positions 0–28. Rune index i has Gematria Primus value p_(i+1). Confusing these conventions introduces an off-by-one error.

Which way does the lookup go?

There are two different questions: “Which prime is in position 3299?” and “What position does the prime 3299 occupy?” Both use the number 3299, but they return different answers. In the first question, 3299 is an index; in the second, it is a value.

	Prime value	Its one-based position	Equivalent statement

	3299	463	p_(463) = 3299

	7649	971	p_(971) = 7649

	9467	1173	p_(1173) = 9467

	30557	3299	p_(3299) = 30557

	98597	9467	p_(9467) = 98597


For example, replacing the prime value 3299 with its position gives 463. Treating 3299 as a position and looking up the prime there gives 30557. “Take the prime ordinal” is ambiguous unless the direction is stated. The input to an nth-prime lookup need not itself be prime: p_(4) = 7 is perfectly well-defined, although 4 is composite.

The prime-counting function π(x) counts primes less than or equal to x. For a prime q, π(q) is its one-based position. For a composite x, π(x) still exists, but it is not the ordinal of x as a prime. Here π is a function name, not the circle constant.

The 3299 and 9467 examples
The decimal number 3299 appears in red on LP2-15. The arithmetic lookups p_(3299) = 30,557 and p_(9467) = 98,597 are exact. Their product is:
98597 × 30557 = 3012828529
 9857 × 30557 =  301200349
The second expression omits a 9 and gives a different answer. Preserve the operands as well as the final sequence when describing a hypothesis. These calculations establish arithmetic, not a relationship between manuscript pages.

LP2-15: the complete number panel, heading, and drawing.

Turning the product into a sequence is another decision

The product is an integer. Reading it as ten separate decimal digits, as five two-digit groups, or as a source of rune shifts gives different inputs. If you choose single digits and add consecutive primes, the first four sums are:

Product digits:     3  0  1  2
Consecutive primes: 2  3  5  7
Sums:               5  3  6  9

Using 0 instead of 7 at the fourth position changes that last sum from 9 to 2. Zero is a valid zero-based rune index for F, but it is not a prime. Such a replacement needs a separate, consistently applied rule: which F positions trigger it, whether they consume a prime, and whether the output is copied or transformed. The interruptions guide explains these alternatives.

Similarly, applying these sums modulo 29 is an additional operation, and applying them as shifts to ciphertext is different from interpreting them directly as rune indices. Write each step explicitly before judging whether the output looks meaningful. A change introduced to improve one fragment must be recorded and checked across the declared scope.

The complete ten-position calculation

Fix one rule: read the product’s decimal digits from left to right and add consecutive primes beginning at 2, without skipping, resetting or replacing any prime. This produces:

	Position	Digit	Prime	Sum

	1	3	2	5

	2	0	3	3

	3	1	5	6

	4	2	7	9

	5	8	11	19

	6	2	13	15

	7	8	17	25

	8	5	19	24

	9	2	23	25

	10	9	29	38


If a separate rule reduces those sums modulo 29, the sequence becomes 5, 3, 6, 9, 19, 15, 25, 24, 25, 9. Only the final sum changes: 38 mod 29 = 9. These residues could be interpreted as direct rune indices or as shifts applied to a specified ciphertext stream, but those are different operations. No ciphertext has been used in this table.

The reproduction script includes the digits, primes, sums and residues in product_digit_prime_addition. This provides a fixed arithmetic reference against which to describe another variant, including an F-triggered exception. It does not fill in the unspecified route from the drawing to 7649 or demonstrate a connection between pages.

How to replicate
python scripts/check_number_examples.py
Run with Python 3 from the repository or extracted reference-data ZIP. The script enumerates primes by exact trial division and checks both lookup directions and the products. Its JSON field prime_value_to_one_based_position reproduces the table above. It makes no network calls or model requests. See emirps and reversal for a distinct operation, and documenting scope before proposing a decoding chain.

Sources
Original page and provenance · Arithmetic source code. Prime notation is a mathematical definition; the page’s printed number does not itself specify this lookup operation.

Emirps and decimal reversal

Check reversed primes without conflating reversal, mirroring, and prime lookup.

An emirp is a prime whose decimal digits, reversed, form a different prime. Both primality and the difference condition matter. This is a property of a number’s decimal representation, not a cipher by itself.

Examples and non-examples
13 and 31 form an emirp pair. 11 is prime but palindromic, so it is not an emirp under this definition. 23 is prime, but its reverse 32 is composite. The pair 7649 and 9467 passes both prime checks.
Keep decimal reversal distinct from mirroring an image, reversing rune order, complementing digits, and taking a prime ordinal. Decimal reversal of 8734 is 4378. A transformation from 8734 to 7649 therefore needs a separately specified rule; “invert” alone does not define it.

Where this matters in the manuscript
The spelling and prime-sum article computes the three LP2-57 body sentence totals under a declared rune-only convention and checks their reversals. The boundaries and counting convention belong to the claim. Finding an emirp after changing a boundary is a different test.

The infinity character and 8734

The Unicode Mathematical Operators chart lists the infinity character as U+221E. The digits after U+ are hexadecimal: E represents fourteen. Converting the code point to decimal gives:

0x221E = 2 × 16³ + 2 × 16² + 1 × 16 + 14 = 8734

That conversion is exact for the Unicode character ∞. Choosing that character to represent the open crossed-loop drawing on LP2-15 is a separate hypothesis. A picture in a JPEG does not inherently have a Unicode code point, even when it resembles a familiar symbol.

	Specified operation	Result

	Convert hexadecimal 221E to decimal	8734

	Reverse the decimal digits of 8734	4378

	Replace each decimal digit d with 9 − d	1265

	Negate the integer 8734	−8734

	Reverse the decimal digits of 7649	9467


These are different operations, although several might informally be called “inverting.” None of the first four gives 7649. A proposed route from 8734 to 7649 therefore needs its own explicit transformation; the fact that 7649 and 9467 are both prime does not supply that missing step.

A code point is not a byte sequence

The same infinity character has code-point value 8734 and UTF-8 bytes E2 88 9E. The former is a number assigned to the character; the latter is one encoding of it. Reversing decimal digits, reversing hexadecimal characters, and reversing encoded bytes are distinct tests. Always record which representation is being used before applying a numerical operation.

This Python 3 check reproduces the character conversion, byte encoding, and two decimal transformations without any external package:

symbol = "\u221e"
value = ord(symbol)
reverse = int(str(value)[::-1])
complement = "".join(str(9 - int(d)) for d in str(value))
print(value)                          # 8734
print(symbol.encode("utf-8").hex(" ")) # e2 88 9e
print(reverse)                        # 4378
print(complement)                     # 1265
assert value == int("221E", 16) == 8734
assert reverse == 4378
assert complement == "1265"

For the later, independently checkable steps of the 301 calculation, see the two nth-prime lookups and their product. Keeping a correct multiplication separate from an unspecified earlier transformation makes the hypothesis easier to investigate.

How to replicate the predicate
from math import isqrt
def prime(n):
    return n >= 2 and all(n % d for d in range(2, isqrt(n) + 1))
def emirp(n):
    reverse = int(str(n)[::-1]) if n >= 0 else -1
    return n != reverse and prime(n) and prime(reverse)
assert emirp(7649)
assert not emirp(11)
Converting the reversed digits to an integer removes leading zeros. This convention must be stated if applying reversal to strings that are not already prime numbers. See prime indices and selection effects.

Reproducing rune prime sums provides a read-only command and explicit spelling comparisons.
Sources and evidence
Exact sentence sums and conventions · Checked numerical examples. No authorial purpose follows from the emirp property alone.

  https://jelliottdev.github.io/reference/articles/mobius.html

  https://jelliottdev.github.io/reference/articles/prime-indices.html#examples

  https://jelliottdev.github.io/reference/articles/prime-indices.html

  https://jelliottdev.github.io/reference/articles/reproducibility.html
- Reproducing rune prime sums
  https://jelliottdev.github.io/reference/articles/prime-sums.html

Magic squares in the 2014 puzzle

Convert LP1-05 rune words into the 1033 square, check LP1-16’s 3301 square, and distinguish both from the embedded grids and LP2-15 panel.

A magic square has equal sums in every row, every column, and both main diagonals. Its order is its width and height; its magic constant is that common sum. Equal row sums alone are not enough.

Which number grid are you looking for?
	Location	What is present	What is checked
	LP1-05	Five-by-five grid of numbers and rune words	After rune-value substitution, all twelve lines sum to 1033
	LP1-16	Five-by-five grid of printed numbers	All twelve lines sum to 3301 directly
	LP1-10–13 embedded messages	ASCII grids with differing borders	The displayed three-by-three interior alone is not magic
	LP2-15	Four-by-four decimal panel, with red 3299	Printed rows and columns have unequal sums
	LP2-49–51	Two-character letter-and-number entries between plant borders	256 entries in eight-column arrays; no numeral base assumed
These are different objects. Specify the page, whether the grid is visible or extracted, and any substitution before comparing totals.
Magic does not always mean normal
A normal order-n magic square uses each integer from 1 to n² exactly once. A general magic square need not use that range or distinct entries. Keep the definition separate from any additional rules in a historical challenge.

LP1-05: turning rune words into a 1033 square
The Some Wisdom page, LP1-05, prints a five-by-five grid containing both decimal numbers and rune words below CNOW THIS. The all-number version recorded in the historical walkthrough is a conversion of that mixed grid. Keep each printed number unchanged; replace each rune word with the sum of its Gematria Primus prime values.
[Image: LP1-05: red heading above a grid containing decimal numbers and rune words.]
Original-image detail, rectangle [500, 1900, 1400, 900]. Complete page · Original JPEG.
The resulting matrix is:
272 138 341 131 151
366 199 130 320  18
226 245  91 245 226
 18 320 130 199 366
151 131 341 138 272
All five rows, all five columns, and both diagonals sum to 1033. Entries repeat, so it is not a normal square. This is historical context, not a newly discovered Liber Primus solution.

Every rune cell, worked through
Row and column positions below start at 1. Latin labels identify the original runes; a multi-letter label can still represent one rune. Sum the listed prime values once each. Do not replace the unusual spellings with ordinary English or sum Unicode character numbers.
	Row, column	Rune labels	Prime values	Total
	1, 3	SHADOWS	53 + 23 + 97 + 89 + 7 + 19 + 53	341
	2, 1	AETHEREAL	101 + 5 + 67 + 11 + 109 + 73	366
	2, 2	BUFFERS	61 + 3 + 2 + 2 + 67 + 11 + 53	199
	2, 3	UOID	3 + 7 + 31 + 89	130
	2, 4	CARNAL	13 + 97 + 11 + 29 + 97 + 73	320
	3, 2	OBSCURA	7 + 61 + 53 + 13 + 3 + 11 + 97	245
	3, 3	FORM	2 + 7 + 11 + 71	91
	3, 5	MOBIUS	71 + 7 + 61 + 31 + 3 + 53	226
	4, 2	ANALOG	97 + 29 + 97 + 73 + 7 + 17	320
	4, 3	UOID	3 + 7 + 31 + 89	130
	4, 4	MOURNFUL	71 + 7 + 3 + 11 + 29 + 2 + 3 + 73	199
	4, 5	AETHEREAL	101 + 5 + 67 + 11 + 109 + 73	366
	5, 3	CABAL	13 + 97 + 61 + 97 + 73	341
For example, the top-row rune word gives 341. The first row then becomes 272 + 138 + 341 + 131 + 151 = 1033. The complete reading places the grid beside the statements about primes and the totient function; those statements and this additive conversion are related context, not interchangeable arithmetic operations.
Run python scripts/check_number_examples.py from the repository folder. Its lp1_05 result includes every rune cell, the converted matrix, all twelve line sums, and input hashes. The script reads the page and alphabet records and checks that the conversion equals the historical numeric example. Unknown symbols cause an error rather than being silently discarded.
Equal sums do not mean matching words
Turn the converted LP1-05 number grid through 180 degrees and every value matches its opposite. Do the same with the printed tokens and five of the twelve opposite pairs differ. The remaining seven pairs match exactly; the center cell stays in place. Here are the five differences, using one-based row and column positions:
	Printed token	Opposite token	Value
	SHADOWS
Row 1, col 3	CABAL
Row 5, col 3	341
	BUFFERS
Row 2, col 2	MOURNFUL
Row 4, col 4	199
	CARNAL
Row 2, col 4	ANALOG
Row 4, col 2	320
	226
Row 3, col 1	MOBIUS
Row 3, col 5	226
	OBSCURA
Row 3, col 2	245
Row 3, col 4	245
The word pairs SHADOWS/CABAL, BUFFERS/MOURNFUL and CARNAL/ANALOG have equal additive rune values despite having different rune sequences. The other two pairs put a decimal number opposite a rune word. Thus the symmetry belongs to the converted values, not to identical writing in every opposite cell.
This is an example of a sum collision: different inputs produce the same total. Addition also loses order, so rearranging the same runes leaves their sum unchanged. A total therefore cannot uniquely recover a word, establish that two words mean the same thing, or specify a decoding rule. The spelling and prime-sum guide explains why word order and rune choice must be kept separate when evaluating unusual spellings.
To reproduce this distinction, run python scripts/check_number_examples.py and inspect lp1_05.half_turn_pairs. Each pair records its positions, Latin labels, whether its original tokens match, and its converted values. The output reports printed_tokens_half_turn_symmetric: false and converted_values_half_turn_symmetric: true. The first comparison is between stored tokens, not a pixel-by-pixel test of the handwriting.
The printed 3301 square on LP1-16

The final LP1 sheet contains a five-by-five decimal square below the heading read as CNOW THIS. These are printed numbers, not prime values calculated from runes. The complete instruction reading preserves their position after the text and insect illustration.

[Image: LP1-16 detail: the red heading above five rows of decimal numbers.]
Original-image detail, rectangle [500, 1800, 1400, 900]. Complete page · Original JPEG.

 434 1311 312  278  966
 204  812 934  280 1071
 626  620 809  620  626
1071  280 934  812  204
 966  278 312 1311  434

Every row, every column and both main diagonals sum to 3301. For example, the first row gives 434 + 1311 + 312 + 278 + 966 = 3301; the descending diagonal gives 434 + 812 + 809 + 812 + 434 = 3301. The total of all 25 entries is 16505, which is five times the common line sum. The square is magic under the definition above, but not normal: it repeats values and does not use 1 through 25.

It also has half-turn symmetry: rotate the grid through 180 degrees and every entry returns to an equal entry. In zero-based coordinates, A[r][c] = A[4-r][4-c]. The center, 809, stays in place. This is different from reflecting only left-to-right: the first row reversed is the last row, not the first row. Symmetry and equal sums are separate properties, so both should be checked.

Reproduce the calculation

From the repository folder, run python scripts/check_number_examples.py. No extra packages, network access or AI service are needed. The script reads the five decimal rows directly from the page transcription, checks all twelve line sums and the half-turn, and prints a JSON result under lp1_16. It also records the transcription file hash and the original image hash so another researcher can identify the inputs.

row_sums:      [3301, 3301, 3301, 3301, 3301]
column_sums:   [3301, 3301, 3301, 3301, 3301]
diagonal_sums: [3301, 3301]
total: 16505
half_turn_symmetric: true
normal: false

Download the calculation script. Run it inside the repository so its page-record path resolves. The script verifies arithmetic from the stored transcription; checking those digits against the original JPEG is the independent visual step. These results do not establish that the square supplies a key for an unsolved page or reproduces a historical server submission.

The later LP1 payloads
LP1-10 through LP1-13 contain signed instructions referring to three magic squares. Their ASCII borders differ. If one removes the surrounding border digits, the displayed interior is:
10 12 10
12 14 12
10 12 10
Its row sums are 32, 38, and 32. It is not itself a magic square under the definition above. Do not label the visible number arrangement as a solved magic square merely because the surrounding prose mentions them.
The historical walkthrough later describes an input form accepting squares subject to criteria, with an order-5 square summing to 3301 as one example. This wiki has not independently reconstructed the historical server validator. That report does not prove that the earlier 1033 square was the required submission.

The LP2-15 decimal panel is another distinct arrangement; its printed row and column sums are unequal.
How to check a square

This complete Python 3 example uses the historical arrangement above. It prints row, column, and diagonal totals separately, so a failed check can be located rather than hidden behind a single yes/no result. It needs no files or extra packages.

square = [
    [272, 138, 341, 131, 151],
    [366, 199, 130, 320, 18],
    [226, 245, 91, 245, 226],
    [18, 320, 130, 199, 366],
    [151, 131, 341, 138, 272],
]
n = len(square)
assert n and all(len(row) == n for row in square)
rows = [sum(row) for row in square]
columns = [sum(row[c] for row in square) for c in range(n)]
diagonals = [sum(square[i][i] for i in range(n)),
             sum(square[i][n - 1 - i] for i in range(n))]
lines = rows + columns + diagonals
is_magic = len(set(lines)) == 1
entries = [value for row in square for value in row]
is_normal = is_magic and sorted(entries) == list(range(1, n * n + 1))
print("Rows:", rows)
print("Columns:", columns)
print("Diagonals:", diagonals)
print("Magic:", is_magic, "Normal:", is_normal)
assert lines == [1033] * 12
assert is_magic and not is_normal

Expected output:

Rows: [1033, 1033, 1033, 1033, 1033]
Columns: [1033, 1033, 1033, 1033, 1033]
Diagonals: [1033, 1033]
Magic: True Normal: False

The repository command python scripts/check_number_examples.py checks the same twelve lines alongside the recorded prime-number examples. Either calculation checks arithmetic, not provenance or historical server acceptance.

Where the magic constant comes from

If an order-n square has row sum M, adding all rows gives a total of nM. Thus the total of all entries divided by n is the only possible common row sum. For this example, the total is 5165, so the candidate is 5165 / 5 = 1033. That is a necessary condition, not a substitute for checking the individual lines.

For a normal square, the sum of the integers 1 through n² is n²(n² + 1) / 2. Dividing by n gives the familiar constant n(n² + 1) / 2. A normal order-5 square therefore has constant 65. Applying that formula to this non-normal historical arrangement would be a category error: it does not contain the integers 1 through 25.

Symmetry is a different property

The three-by-three interior in the signed payload looks balanced because it repeats under horizontal and vertical reflection. But its outer rows total 32 while its middle row totals 38. Its columns likewise total 32, 38, and 32; both main diagonals total 34. The total of all entries is 102, giving a candidate constant of 34, yet not one row reaches that value.

	Check	Historical 5 × 5	Payload interior 3 × 3

	All row sums equal?	Yes: 1033	No: 32, 38, 32

	All column sums equal?	Yes: 1033	No: 32, 38, 32

	Both main diagonals match that sum?	Yes: 1033	Both are 34, but the rows and columns fail

	Magic under the stated definition?	Yes	No


A centered layout, repeated numbers, or matching diagonals can be worth describing without calling the arrangement magic. The LP2-15 panel guide applies this same separation between visible pattern and checked sums to its sixteen printed values.

Sources
Pinned 2014 walkthrough · LP1-10 body · All signed payloads and hashes.


Looking for the letter-and-number arrays between plant borders? See LP2-49–51’s alphanumeric grids. Their rectangular layout alone does not make them magic squares.

The LP2-56 hash target

The exact printed value, its representation, and the assumptions a candidate check must state.

LP2-56 has a known reading titled “An End.” Its text refers to a page in the deep web that hashes to the hexadecimal value printed between the runic passages. Decoding the surrounding runes and finding the referenced page are separate tasks.

The page record separates the printed hexadecimal block from the runic passages and red punctuation. Five large black dots sit below the text; the illustrated dot guide records them independently of the hash.
The literal target
The archived transcription preserves five printed rows:
36367763ab73783c7af284446c
59466b4cd653239a311cb7116
d4618dee09a8425893dc7500b
464fdaf1672d7bef5e891c6e227
4568926a49fb4f45132c2a8b4
Concatenating the rows yields 128 hexadecimal characters, representing 64 bytes, or 512 bits. The rows are presentation breaks; preserving them in a text file is different from the single digest string used for comparison.

Length is evidence of format, not proof of an algorithm
A SHA-512 digest has this length. The quoted decoded instruction does not name SHA-512 or define which bytes of a “page” should be hashed. Length alone cannot distinguish all algorithms that produce 512-bit outputs. State SHA-512 explicitly as an assumption when testing a candidate.
A URL string, an HTTP response body, an HTML source file, rendered text, and a screenshot are different inputs. Their hashes need not agree. Encoding, line endings, compression handling, and trailing newlines also matter. Do not silently normalize a candidate after a mismatch.

Extract the target from the shipped reading
import json, re
from pathlib import Path
page = json.loads(Path("data/pages/lp2-56.json").read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
lines = [line.rstrip("/") for line in page["reading"]["literal"].splitlines()]
rows = [line for line in lines if re.fullmatch(r"[0-9a-f]+", line)]
target = "".join(rows)
assert len(rows) == 5 and len(target) == 128
assert len(bytes.fromhex(target)) == 64
print(target)
This extracts a preserved target. It does not discover a destination, query a network, or test candidate pages. Use the reading recipe to reproduce the surrounding text independently.

Compare a local candidate file
The candidate-file checker makes one explicit assumption: SHA-512 is the algorithm to test. It reads an existing local file as bytes, without parsing HTML, decoding text, changing line endings, or making a network request.
Extract the reference-data bundle and run from that folder, replacing the quoted path with the file you want to check:
python scripts/check_lp2_target.py "candidate.html"
The JSON report includes the file’s byte count, SHA-256 for identifying the tested bytes, computed SHA-512, preserved target digest, and matches. It also records the hash of the page record from which the target was extracted. The script reads the candidate and prints the report; it does not modify either source file.
	Exit status	Meaning
	0	The computed SHA-512 equals the target.
	1	The exact tested bytes do not match under SHA-512.
	2	The input could not be read or the target record was invalid; no comparison result was produced.
An exit status of 1 is an ordinary mismatch, not a script malfunction. A report identifies what was hashed, but cannot supply missing provenance: record where the candidate came from, when it was obtained, and how it was saved. A browser’s saved HTML and a captured response body may contain different bytes even when they display similarly.
Record exactly what a candidate check establishes
A mismatch excludes the tested bytes under the chosen algorithm. It does not exclude every version of a site, every serialization, or every algorithm. A reported match should include the exact candidate bytes, their provenance, the hashing operation, and an independently repeatable comparison. See checksums and reproducibility.

Sources and status
Original image and reading · Structured record · Pinned walkthrough. The source snapshot establishes the known reading; this article does not assert that the referenced page has been located.

The LP2-15 number panel and heading

The exact 4 × 4 matrix, checked totals, red entry, heading, and open-loop drawing.

LP2-15 contains a red runic heading, a 4 × 4 decimal panel, and an open-loop drawing below it. Its combined archive index is 32. Use the release ID when citing it: LP1-15 is a different image with a known keyed reading.

[Image: Detail of LP2-15 showing the red runic heading, all sixteen numbers and the crossed-loop drawing]
Cropped view of LP2-15, retaining the page’s orientation and colors. Compare the four rows with the transcription below; the complete sheet remains available in the original file. Complete original JPEG · Download
The exact number panel
Values in image order; row and column positions are one-based here.
	Row	Column 1	Column 2	Column 3	Column 4

	1	3258	3222	3152	3038

	2	3278	3299 (red)	3298	2838

	3	3288	3294	3296	2472

	4	4516	1206	708	1820

3299 is the only red number. 708 is the only three-digit entry. Preserve 4516 as printed; its being larger than 3301 is not a reason to change it. The structured page record stores the matrix in its numbers field.

Straightforward arithmetic
The row sums are 12670, 12713, 12350, and 8250. The column sums are 14340, 11021, 10454, and 10168. The two main diagonals sum to 11673 and 14146. All sixteen entries sum to 45983.
These unequal totals mean that the printed panel is not a magic square under the ordinary equal-line-sums definition. This says nothing about a proposed transformation of the entries; a transformed panel would be a different object and require its own stated rule.

Subtracting the entries from 3301

Choose the explicit operation d = 3301 − printed entry, keeping all sixteen positions. The resulting panel is:

Derived differences, not numbers printed on the page
	Row	Column 1	Column 2	Column 3	Column 4

	1	43	79	149	263

	2	23	2	3	463

	3	13	7	5	829

	4	−1215	2095	2593	1481


Fourteen differences are prime. All twelve entries in the first three rows are prime, as are the final two entries of the fourth row. The exceptions are 3301 − 4516 = −1215, which is negative and therefore not prime, and 3301 − 1206 = 2095 = 5 × 419, which is composite.

The red 3299 gives a difference of 2, the first prime. The entry 2838 gives 463; separately, 3299 is the 463rd prime. These are checkable numerical relationships. They do not establish that the page instructs either subtraction or an ordinal lookup. See the two directions of a prime lookup.

Using an absolute value, changing a printed entry, or dropping the last row would define a different procedure. Keep the full panel when describing this one. Counting fourteen primes is a descriptive result; judging how surprising it is requires a stated comparison model and an account of how the constant and operation were selected.

Download all sixteen positions as CSV · Download the matrix and checks as JSON. The CSV keeps the printed value and derived difference in separate columns. Row and column coordinates start at one in the image’s original orientation; difference_is_prime is explicitly true or false. Each row also records the operation and source hashes. Sort entire rows to keep those fields together.

Reproduce the difference panel

python scripts/check_number_examples.py

The output’s lp2_15 object includes the source-record hash, original-image hash, printed matrix, transformed matrix and a Boolean prime flag for each position. Primality is checked by exact trial division through the integer square root. Run from the repository or extracted reference-data bundle with Python 3. The script reads the stored panel and does not modify it or execute a cipher search.

The heading is not a known plaintext
[Image: Red LP2-15 heading with dot clusters at either end and a separator between its two rune groups]
Heading detail from the original image. The terminal dot clusters and the separator between groups are visible alongside the runes. Complete original JPEG · Download
The recorded heading has nine runes in groups of four and five: F U L M / A EA Y OE A. EA and OE each label a single rune. These are transliteration labels, not an English translation. The source snapshot does not establish “CRYING” or another plaintext for this heading.

The drawing below the panel
[Image: Black two-lobed drawing beneath the LP2-15 number panel, with two open ends near the center]
Drawing detail from the original image. Inspect the open ends near the center rather than substituting a typeset infinity symbol. Complete original JPEG · Download
The page annotation describes two open lobes with a crossing, resembling an infinity sign; visible gaps remain. Shape resemblance does not establish that the author intended a particular Unicode character, its code point, or a numerical transformation of that code point. Keep the observed drawing separate from those proposed operations.

How to reproduce the totals
import json
from pathlib import Path
p = json.loads(Path("data/pages/lp2-15.json").read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
a = p["numbers"]
assert len(a) == 4 and all(len(row) == 4 for row in a)
print("rows", [sum(row) for row in a])
print("columns", [sum(row[c] for row in a) for c in range(4)])
print("diagonals", sum(a[i][i] for i in range(4)),
      sum(a[i][3-i] for i in range(4)))
print("total", sum(map(sum, a)))
This is a check of the published transcription, not a cipher experiment or a new image audit. Compare the matrix to the original in the reader before using it as an input.

Following a numerical idea
The prime-index guide checks the arithmetic involving 3299, 30557, 9467, and 98597. The emirp guide distinguishes decimal reversal from mirroring and unspecified “inversion.” A valid calculation does not by itself connect LP2-15 with LP2-00–02. Record that proposed connection as a hypothesis with explicit operations and scope.

Sources
Original image, annotations, and archive provenance · Pinned number and rune transcription. Visual observations follow the existing page annotations; the totals above are derived arithmetic.

The two LP1 title pages

Visible Latin headings, the meaning of Intus, and the hidden-message chain.

Looking for the cover with compasses? See the illustrated cover and its Blake artwork. It is separate from the title pages discussed here.

The first release includes two title images among its seventeen pages. They are part of the file sequence and the hidden-message chain, even though neither has a runic paragraph.


[Image: Cropped preview of the Latin title Liber Primus on LP1-00]
LP1-00 · Liber Primus. Preview of the visible lettering; open the reader to inspect the complete page and margins.

[Image: Cropped preview showing Chapter 1 above Intus on LP1-02]
LP1-02 · Chapter 1 — Intus. The gap between the two text groups is visible in this preview.


These cropped previews help identify the pages; they are not the files used for OutGuess extraction. Use the LP1-00 original download and LP1-02 original download for byte-level work.

LP1-00: Liber Primus
The cover displays “Liber Primus” in large black Latin lettering on a white field. The text sits above the vertical midpoint with broad margins. The literal visible text is recorded separately from the archived rune transcriptions; a rune count of zero does not mean the image contains no text or no information.

LP1-02: Chapter 1 — Intus
The chapter title displays “Chapter 1” above “Intus,” in black Latin lettering on white. The two text groups are vertically separated. In Latin, intus can mean “within” or “on the inside”; see the Lewis and Short dictionary entry. That lexical meaning does not by itself specify a cipher operation.

Both carry hidden messages
Each original JPEG yields a signed hexadecimal OutGuess body. Together with the warning image, LP1-01, they form the three-image XOR and transposition chain. Their visible headings and embedded bodies must remain separate in transcriptions and citations.

How to inspect the layers
Open the original image in the reader and compare its visible lettering with the labeled visible-text transcription.
Download the original JPEG, not the cropped thumbnail.
Follow OutGuess extraction and compare the expected checksum.
Verify the signed block, then follow the documented three-image chain.
The site’s title-page text is a labeled editorial transcription checked against the image on 19 October 2026. It is not a new cipher reading or a replacement for the image.

Sources
LP1-00 original and file provenance · LP1-02 original and file provenance · Hidden-payload evidence. Visual descriptions concern the displayed originals; no font identification or numerical interpretation of the layout is asserted.

The image hidden in LP1-03

The decoded JPEG, its archived rune transcription, and exact reproduction steps.

LP1-03 has two different images to examine: the visible runic manuscript page and a smaller JPEG encoded inside its signed OutGuess message. The known Vigenère reading of the manuscript does not automatically decode the second image.

Four layers to keep separate

	Layer	What you examine
	Original LP1-03 JPEG	The visible Welcome page, with its runes and leafy border. It also carries hidden data.
	OutGuess payload	31,809 extracted bytes containing the signed message.
	Signed message body	A short instruction followed by hexadecimal text representing another JPEG.
	Decoded JPEG	The small rune-and-digit image shown below, 15,188 bytes long.

The body opens with “Let the text guide you.”, then “Good luck.” and “3301”, before the hexadecimal sequence. These words are in the extracted message, not the visible runic paragraph on the manuscript sheet. Read the complete body or inspect the signed block.

OutGuess extraction, signature verification, and hexadecimal decoding answer different questions. Extraction retrieves the stored bytes. Signature verification checks the signed content against a particular public key. Hexadecimal decoding converts character pairs into bytes. None of those operations alone supplies a reading of the runes in the resulting image.

The decoded derivative
[Image: A narrow black rune sequence containing the decimal digits 5 and 3 on a white background]
The JPEG decoded from the hexadecimal portion of LP1-03’s signed message.
The derivative is 587 × 109 pixels and 15,188 bytes. Download the JPEG. Its checksum is recorded in the payload manifest.

Archived transcription
The pinned iBotPeaches archive supplies this transcription:
ᚦᛗᛞᛇᚠᛗᚪᚱ5ᚢᚫᛝᚱᛝ3 ᛠᛗᛇᚠᛡ
It contains 18 runes and the decimal digits 5 and 3. In the wiki’s alphabet labels, with spaces inserted between individual symbols for clarity:
TH M D EO F M A R 5 U AE NG R NG 3 EA M EO F IA
Those labels are a transliteration, not established plaintext. The added spaces above identify symbol boundaries; they are not a new claim about word boundaries in the image. Decimal digits remain digits rather than becoming rune indices.

How to reproduce the image
First follow OutGuess extraction for LP1-03 and verify its signed message. Decode the hexadecimal suffix of the exported body:
import hashlib
import json
from pathlib import Path

manifest = json.loads(
    Path("data/evidence/embedded-payloads.json").read_text(encoding="utf-8")
)
record = next(row for row in manifest["records"] if row["page"] == "lp1-03")
body_bytes = Path(record["body_path"]).read_bytes()
if hashlib.sha256(body_bytes).hexdigest() != record["body_sha256"]:
    raise ValueError("Message body differs from the recorded source")
body = body_bytes.decode("utf-8")
image = bytes.fromhex(body[body.index("ffd8ffe"):])
if len(image) != record["embedded_image_bytes"]:
    raise ValueError("Decoded JPEG length differs from the record")
if hashlib.sha256(image).hexdigest() != record["embedded_image_sha256"]:
    raise ValueError("Decoded JPEG differs from the recorded derivative")
with open("lp1-03-decoded.jpg", "xb") as output:
    output.write(image)
print("Verified and wrote", len(image), "bytes")
The exclusive-create mode refuses to overwrite an existing file. This reproduces a format conversion, not a proposed solution to the image’s text. Keep the original signed body and the derivative as separate files.

Run the example from an extracted reference-data bundle or the repository root. It uses only Python’s standard library. A successful run prints Verified and wrote 15188 bytes. The hashes check consistency with the supplied manifest; authenticate the signed message separately using the linked verification instructions.
If a hash check fails, stop before interpreting the derivative. Confirm that the message body and manifest come from the same download, and avoid opening and resaving the body in an editor that changes line endings. Use the file-verification guide to compare bytes. The checks deliberately read the body as bytes before decoding its text.
Sources
Pinned transcription of the embedded image · Signed block · Message body · Payload inventory.

LP2-00–02: text and image measurements

Cross-like margin drawings, loops, the insect, and measured rune and punctuation regions on the opening pages.

LP2-00, LP2-01, and LP2-02 are the first three images of the second release. Their combined archive indices are 17–19. The source snapshot does not give them a known plaintext. Studying them together does not establish a shared key or a reset rule.

[Image: LP2-00 manuscript preview]
LP2-00 · Read
[Image: LP2-01 manuscript preview]
LP2-01 · Read
[Image: LP2-02 manuscript preview]
LP2-02 · Read
Crosses, loops, and the insect

All three pages place one cross-like drawing high in the right margin and another lower in the left margin. Each has a long stem crossed by three bars. The broadest bar is near the upper end of the right-hand drawing and the lower end of the left-hand drawing. This makes the pair useful to compare, but visual resemblance alone does not establish that one is an exact rotation of the other.

	Page	Beyond the margin drawings	Inspect

	LP2-00	Small two-lobed loops above and below the text.	Page 00 notes

	LP2-01	A loop above the text, without a corresponding loop below the final row.	Page 01 notes

	LP2-02	A winged insect-like drawing below the text, with its head to the right and a striped wing extending left.	Page 02 notes


The labels “cross,” “signpost,” and “infinity” describe resemblances. They do not settle a religious identification, a direction to read the runes, or an arithmetic operation. For comparison with other pages, see insect imagery and the larger crossed loop on LP2-15. A proposed connection should identify the exact drawings and what feature is being compared.

What has been measured
	Page	Rune regions	Red runes	Dark runes	Punctuation regions

	LP2-00	262	13	249	58

	LP2-01	266	0	266	62

	LP2-02	201	0	201	38

These are 729 stored rune regions and 158 punctuation regions. A region is a measurement unit, not necessarily a separate linguistic character. Rune counts refer to the archived transcription and its mapped image regions.

Punctuation has its own color and shape
LP2-00 has 56 one-component punctuation regions, one four-component region, and one thirteen-component region. One of its one-component marks and its thirteen-component mark are classified red. LP2-01 has 57 one-component and five four-component regions, all dark. LP2-02 has 36 one-component regions, one four-component region, and one thirteen-component region; the thirteen-component region is red.
Thus LP2-02 has no red rune regions but does have red punctuation. The recorded component count describes connected foreground pixels under a threshold, not the number of sentences, cipher shifts, or semantic separators. See image regions and connected components.

Layout details that affect inspection
LP2-00’s oversized opening S rune extends alongside the first three text rows. Its stored rectangle is [599, 664, 153, 501] in original-image pixels. Treating each horizontal row as independent can miss that shared visual context.
LP2-01’s recorded tenth visual row contains C/OE glyphs touching at their feet. Overlapping inspection rectangles preserve their context. A touching shape does not automatically merge the two transcription symbols.

Do not equate transcript punctuation with pixel shape
The archived ASCII notation can use the same period character for marks with different visual component counts. A period in exported text therefore does not prove that every corresponding mark has the same appearance. Keep transcription conventions, image observations, and a proposed reset rule separate.

How to inspect and reproduce the inventory
Open a page record and expand its recorded rune or punctuation regions.
Select “Inspect region” to view the recorded rectangle against the original image.
Use the page JSON’s visual.glyphs and visual.punctuation arrays to inspect the stored data.
Run the checks below from the repository root.
# Structural checks and stored counts; Python standard library:
python scripts/inspect_visual_records.py
# Fresh color/component recount within stored rectangles; requires Pillow:
python scripts/inspect_visual_records.py --pixels
If Pillow is not installed, install it with python -m pip install Pillow in your chosen Python environment. The pixel check verifies the original JPEG hashes before reading them. It does not generate new segmentation, decide which rune a shape represents, or test a cipher.

Evidence and limits
Measurement conventions and checked scope · Reproduction script · LP2-00 source record · LP2-01 source record · LP2-02 source record. Color classes and component counts were reproduced inside the published rectangles on 19 October 2026. This does not make the visual inventory exhaustive or establish a relationship with LP2-15’s number panel.


See also: illustrated index · dots and punctuation · Möbius and the crossed loop.

Image regions and connected components

Understand pixel rectangles, thresholded shapes, and recorded color classes.

An image region specifies where a measurement was made. Keeping the rectangle, original image, and measurement rule together lets another person inspect the same pixels.

Reading a rectangle
The wiki uses [x, y, width, height] in original-image pixels. The origin is the top-left; x increases rightward and y downward. For [599, 664, 153, 501], the region starts at x = 599, y = 664 and covers 153 columns and 501 rows. In a half-open crop convention, the right and bottom bounds are 752 and 1165.
A thumbnail or resized preview uses different display coordinates. Use the original JPEG or the wiki’s region inspector rather than copying screen coordinates into a dataset.

Connected components
A connected component is a group of selected pixels joined by the chosen neighborhood rule. Eight-connectivity includes horizontal, vertical, and diagonal neighbors. Four-connectivity excludes diagonal neighbors; the same image can produce different counts under those definitions.
The published opening-page measurement uses foreground grayscale below 140 and retains eight-connected groups containing at least 20 pixels. Tiny isolated specks are excluded by that area threshold. A count of 13 means thirteen qualifying groups under this rule, not necessarily thirteen intentional dots.

The same pixels, two different counts

In this invented three-by-three mask, # marks a selected foreground pixel and . marks background. It is a teaching example, not a manuscript crop.

# . .
. # .
. . #

	Neighborhood rule	Connections in this mask	Components

	Four-connected	Only shared horizontal or vertical edges count. None of the selected pixels share an edge.	3 components, each of area 1

	Eight-connected	Corner neighbors also connect. The middle pixel connects both outer pixels.	1 component of area 3


Connectivity is transitive: the two outer pixels need not touch each other to belong to the same group. A path through the middle pixel is enough. This is why a thin diagonal bridge can merge what a person sees as separate marks.

Reproduce the small mask

This Python 3 example counts all selected pixels, with no minimum-area filter. It needs no image package:

def component_areas(points, diagonal=False):
    remaining = set(points)
    neighbors = [(1, 0), (-1, 0), (0, 1), (0, -1)]
    if diagonal:
        neighbors += [(1, 1), (1, -1), (-1, 1), (-1, -1)]
    areas = []
    while remaining:
        pending = [remaining.pop()]
        area = 0
        while pending:
            x, y = pending.pop()
            area += 1
            for dx, dy in neighbors:
                neighbor = (x + dx, y + dy)
                if neighbor in remaining:
                    remaining.remove(neighbor)
                    pending.append(neighbor)
        areas.append(area)
    return sorted(areas)

pixels = {(0, 0), (1, 1), (2, 2)}
assert component_areas(pixels) == [1, 1, 1]
assert component_areas(pixels, diagonal=True) == [3]
assert component_areas(set()) == []
print("Four-connected:", component_areas(pixels))
print("Eight-connected:", component_areas(pixels, diagonal=True))

Each selected pixel is removed from the remaining set when it is assigned to a component, so it cannot be counted twice. The reported areas total three under either rule. Connectivity changes grouping, not how many foreground pixels exist.

The real opening-page rule additionally discards components smaller than 20 pixels. Applied to this tiny teaching mask, that filter would retain zero components under either connectivity rule. Always report the neighborhood, brightness threshold and minimum area together; “three dots” is not a complete measurement specification.

Measure the five dots on LP2-56

The five isolated dots below the hash-target text provide a manageable first measurement. The rectangle [800, 2350, 900, 500] contains the dots without the writing above them. Its coordinates refer to the original 2400 by 3600 pixel image.

Download and extract both the reference data and original images into the same directory. Run these commands there, with Python 3 installed:

python -m pip install Pillow
python scripts/measure_region.py lp2-56 --rect 800 2350 900 500 --threshold 140 --minimum-area 20 --connectivity 8

The script checks the original JPEG against the page record’s SHA-256 before decoding it. It converts the pixels to grayscale with Pillow, selects values strictly below 140, groups eight-connected neighbors, and discards groups smaller than 20 pixels. It prints JSON and leaves the image unchanged.

Expected result

With Pillow 11.3.0, the region contains 17,888 selected pixels in five retained components; no small components are discarded. The table lists them from top to bottom by centroid. These row numbers are measurement labels, not a proposed reading order.

	Component	Area in pixels	Centroid (x, y)
	1	3559	1103.934, 2447.301
	2	3560	873.346, 2517.000
	3	3604	1603.870, 2686.500
	4	3542	921.227, 2708.059
	5	3623	1408.122, 2747.286

A centroid is the arithmetic mean of the selected pixels’ x and y indices. It estimates the center of this dark pixel group, not an intended geometric point. The table rounds to three decimal places for readability; the complete JSON result retains six decimals, bounding rectangles, input hash, Pillow version and all measurement settings.

To measure another region, change the page ID and rectangle. Keep the output with your notes, including any settings you change. A rectangle that cuts through a dot measures only the retained part; a threshold that admits a connecting stroke can merge groups. Comparing two patterns also requires a stated rule for matching points and allowing translation, rotation or scaling. Five components alone establish none of those relationships.

Color classification
Within a stored rectangle, foreground pixels use the weighted brightness test 0.299R + 0.587G + 0.114B < 140. A foreground pixel is red-dominant when R − max(G,B) > 70. A red-dominant fraction above 90% gives “red”; below 10% gives “dark”; intermediate cases are “mixed/uncertain.” These labels summarize pixels under a rule, not a chemical analysis of ink.

What a successful recount establishes
Matching a recorded count confirms that the stated operation reproduces it on the stored rectangle and exact image bytes. It does not prove that the rectangle includes every relevant mark or that two overlapping rectangles should be interpreted as one character. Segmentation, symbol identification, and cipher interpretation are separate decisions.

Reproduce the published examples
Follow the LP2-00–02 inventory and run python scripts/inspect_visual_records.py --pixels. The measurement manifest records the scope and input hashes; the script shows the exact implementation. Keep file integrity separate from a claim about meaning.
