Consumption, preservation, and adherence

Read the three behaviors in The Loss of Divinity alongside its advice about wealth, attachment, reason and belonging.

The Loss of Divinity names three behaviors of the circumference: consumption, preservation and adherence. The passage does more than list undesirable actions. It gives motives for them, connects them to a loss of primality, and then follows them with advice about wealth and attachment. Reading those parts together helps explain why its argument is not simply “own nothing” or “reject every belief.”

The source is the complete reading of LP1-10–13. The explanations below paraphrase and interpret that section; they are not additional decoded text or instructions from Liberpedia.

Where each part appears

The argument crosses page boundaries. This map follows the separately recorded literal readings, so it locates the text more precisely than the section’s overall LP1-10–13 range.

	Page	What to look for

	LP1-10	The heading, the three-behavior introduction, and consumption’s first error: not having enough.

	LP1-11	Consumption’s second error, its closing qualification, and the opening explanation of preservation.

	LP1-12	Preservation’s closing qualification, the dogma/reason comparison, and the start of the sentence connecting all three behaviors.

	LP1-13	That sentence concludes with primality and divinity. Separate blocks then address wealth and attachment, followed by programming mind and reality.


In particular, the last row of LP1-12 ends with ADHEREN, and LP1-13 begins CE. Join that word before interpreting the sentence. The page break is not the end of the argument. See literal labels and line boundaries when checking the spelling.

The three behaviors and their stated motives

	Behavior	Reason given in the passage	What the criticism concerns

	Consumption	A belief that there is not enough, or that present resources came through luck and cannot be obtained again.	Consuming too much in response to perceived shortage or future inability.

	Preservation	A belief that losing things would leave a person unable to regain them.	Keeping things because of an assumed weakness or dependence.

	Adherence	Following dogma or reason to belong and to be right.	The purpose for following an idea, including the desire for group membership and vindication.


The first two descriptions share a concern about future capability: will the person be able to obtain what they need again? The third changes the object of dependence from things to belonging and correctness. This is an internal structural comparison. It does not establish a psychological diagnosis or an outside philosophical source.

The manuscript makes the two consumption errors visible as a numbered list: red 1 on LP1-10 and red 2 on LP1-11. The second item continues on the next sheet, before the text moves to preservation.

Consumption: quantity matters

The passage criticizes consuming too much and says that most things are not worth consuming. Those qualifications matter. Replacing them with a claim that all consumption is wrong would change the argument. Its focus is the connection it proposes between excess and the beliefs it calls errors within a deception.

Nor does the text establish that scarcity is always imaginary. It presents a view of the circumference’s motivations; it supplies no empirical survey of scarcity, need or human behavior. A close reading can describe that view without accepting it as a universal fact.

Preservation: what is being kept, and why?

Preservation repeats the concern about being unable to recover a loss. The later advice about possessions makes attachment a useful lens for reading this concern. A thing may be retained because it is useful, or because losing it threatens the identity or security built around it. The passage supports examining that distinction, although it does not provide a practical test for separating the two.

There is an apparent tension with the opening warning, which demands that the book’s words and numbers remain unchanged. One possible reconciliation distinguishes preserving a source accurately from holding possessions out of fear. Another reading may leave the tension unresolved. Neither interpretation authorizes silently changing the warning or erasing the later criticism. The knowledge and authority guide discusses preserving evidence while questioning its claims.

Adherence: why both dogma and reason appear

The two alternatives share the same stated purpose: belonging and being right. Removing reason from the comparison would make the passage sound like a criticism only of dogmatic belief. Removing the purpose would make it sound like a rejection of reasoning itself. Both changes would lose part of the recorded argument.

The following claim about belonging and death is stronger than the preceding account of motives. In the wider manuscript, death and the end of self recur alongside emergence. That makes a metaphorical reading available, but does not prove a single intended meaning. It is especially important to distinguish what this text asserts from what the wiki can independently establish.

Why the advice about wealth matters

After connecting the three behaviors to a loss of primality and divinity, the section permits accumulating great wealth while rejecting attachment to what is owned. Its further instruction about readiness to destroy possessions intensifies that contrast. Possession and dependence are therefore not treated as identical.

That sequence complicates both a simple celebration of wealth and a simple demand for poverty. The text does not explain how to judge readiness, what counts as attachment, or whether its severe language is literal or rhetorical. Those remain questions for interpretation, not missing details to supply as established facts.

“Program your mind. Program reality.”

The closing instruction on LP1-13 follows the advice about wealth and attachment. Its literal labels read PROGRAM-YOU/R-MIND.PROGRAM-REALITY., where the slash marks the archived line break within YOUR. The two short sentences use the same imperative verb, first with mind and then with reality.

[Image: LP1-13, showing the end of the argument and separate Some Wisdom and An Instruction blocks]
LP1-13: read the closing argument, advice, and instruction in order. Open the full page to inspect their separation.

In this context, one possible reading is a shift from diagnosing dependence to asking the reader to exercise agency. The earlier paragraphs describe beliefs about scarcity, weakness, and belonging; the closing command can be read as an invitation to examine and change those patterns. Extending the verb from mind to reality broadens the ambition of the command, but the passage does not explain how that extension is supposed to work.

The wording supplies no program, algorithm, or demonstrated mechanism for changing the external world. It could concern habits, interpretation, action, or a more expansive metaphysical claim; the decoded sentences alone do not decide among those possibilities. A proposed connection to a named psychological practice or philosophical tradition needs evidence beyond the shared word “program.”

Compare the later LP1-16 instruction, which directs inquiry inward and says to impose nothing on others. Reading these instructions together makes the distinction between self-direction and control of other people worth examining. It does not turn either passage into a complete practical method. The knowledge and authority guide follows that distinction across the known readings.

Find and compare the wording

python scripts/reading_concordance.py consumption --json
python scripts/reading_concordance.py preservation --json
python scripts/reading_concordance.py adherence --json
python scripts/reading_concordance.py "belong and be right" --json

The concordance searches contextual English and preserves exact source excerpts in its JSON results. For literal spelling, rune counts or arithmetic, use the complete reading and its reproduction instructions instead. A section’s page range does not place every phrase on every page.

It makes no attribution to Buddhism, Stoicism, Emerson or another tradition merely because a theme is similar. See works and possible influences for the evidence needed to make a source comparison, and philosophical themes for the surrounding manuscript passages.

Search the known readings: a concordance

Find words and phrases in contextual sections or on exact decoded pages, with original excerpts, line locations, and source hashes.

A concordance locates a word or phrase and shows its surrounding text. By default, this tool searches the nine contextual known-reading sections in Liberpedia. Use --literal to locate decoded labels on individual manuscript pages. Both modes help compare recurring terms without relying on memory or repeatedly opening every section.

Run a lookup

Extract the reference-data ZIP, keep its folders together, and run these commands from the extracted directory with Python 3. No extra Python package, network connection, or AI service is needed.

python scripts/reading_concordance.py circumference
python scripts/reading_concordance.py circumference --prefix
python scripts/reading_concordance.py "voice inside your head"
python scripts/reading_concordance.py instar --context 15

Exact search matches whole words or contiguous word sequences, ignoring case and most punctuation. Prefix search accepts one word and matches words that begin with it. Thus circumference --prefix includes the plural, while an exact query does not. Internal apostrophes are retained, so DON'T stays one word; a typographic apostrophe is normalized to the same character.

Read the result

Each hit gives a section ID, its page range, a one-based contextual word position, and the matched text in brackets. The surrounding text is limited by --context, which accepts 0–50 words on each side.

loss-of-divinity (lp1-10, lp1-11, lp1-12, lp1-13), word 6
THE LOSS OF DIVINITY THE [CIRCUMFERENCE] PRACTICES THREE BEHAVIORS ...

This shortened example illustrates the output; the command prints its actual context rather than an ellipsis. A section range does not identify the exact page holding the word. Open the complete reading to compare its literal page outputs and original images.

Locate a word on an exact page

A section can span several sheets. To find the page that actually contains a word, search the 17 available literal page readings:

python scripts/reading_concordance.py circumference --literal --prefix
python scripts/reading_concordance.py circumference --literal --prefix --json

The result places the two singular occurrences on LP1-10 and LP1-14, and the plural on LP2-57. Each hit links to its page record and reports its line range in the stored literal reading.

Words can wrap between lines. On LP1-10, the stored text is CIRCU/ followed on the next line by MFERENCE. This mode removes slash markers and carriage-return/newline characters before matching, so the whole word can be found. Hyphens and other punctuation still separate tokens. It does not join different pages, so a phrase split across two sheets requires the contextual section search.

Literal labels retain their spelling: search DIUINITY, not DIVINITY, and UOICE, not VOICE. No U/V expansion, synonym matching, or spelling correction is applied. A label such as TH can represent one rune, so the reported word and character positions must not be treated as rune indices.

In literal JSON output, matched_source retains the original wraps. The offsets index the page record’s reading.literal string, and line_start and line_end count its lines from one. The report includes the path and SHA-256 of every page record searched. These are hashes of the JSON records, not of the manuscript images. This makes the lookup checkable without implying that decoded Latin labels were printed on the original page.

Scope of the default contextual search

	Included	Outside this search
	One contextual English reading for each of nine sections	Unsolved ciphertext, artwork, and OutGuess messages
	Whole-word and contiguous-phrase matches	Synonyms, semantic similarity, and automatic stemming
	Contextual word positions	Rune offsets, literal prime sums, or exact image coordinates

The tool searches each section once. A four-page section is not counted four times. It also does not join the end of one section to the beginning of another when matching a phrase. A zero result means the requested token sequence was not found in this contextual compilation; it says nothing about the unsolved pages.

Contextual English expands or interprets some literal rune labels. A count in this representation is therefore not automatically a count of literal rune sequences. Use rune indices and prime values when working with the actual encoded symbols.

Save a machine-readable result

python scripts/reading_concordance.py circumference --prefix --json
python scripts/reading_concordance.py circumference --prefix --json --output circumference-concordance.json
python scripts/reading_concordance.py circumference --prefix --output circumference-concordance.txt

The JSON output includes the query, matching mode, tokenization rule, source-file SHA-256, and every hit. Add --output to save the result as a UTF-8 file. The command refuses to overwrite an existing file; choose a new name for a later run. A relative filename is saved in your current working directory, so run these commands from the extracted bundle or repository directory.

Use --json for structured results, including exact source excerpts and character positions. Omit it for the readable text report. The filename extension does not select the format: --json does. Without --output, the result is printed in the terminal. A lookup with no matches still produces a valid report with zero occurrences.

The hash identifies the exact contextual compilation searched. It is not a signature or evidence that the contextual rendering is an original manuscript file. Read the checksum guide for that distinction.

Keep the original wording when comparing passages

Search matching ignores case and most punctuation, but those details can matter when discussing a passage. Each JSON hit therefore also includes matched_source, the matched words with their original capitalization, punctuation and whitespace, and source_excerpt, the surrounding words preserved in the same way. “Original” here means the stored contextual reading, not the manuscript’s rune stream.

For example, searching don't stop can match Don’t, STOP. The normalized match is DON'T STOP, while matched_source retains Don’t, STOP. This lets you find a phrase flexibly without silently rewriting it when you inspect the result.

The fields source_start and source_end locate that match inside the section’s reading string. They count Unicode characters from zero, with the end excluded: in Python, reading[source_start:source_end] recovers matched_source. They are not UTF-8 byte offsets or positions on the manuscript image. The excerpt starts at the first included word and ends at the last included word; punctuation between those words is preserved, but punctuation outside those boundaries is not included.

Check the implementation

python scripts/test_reading_concordance.py

The checks cover the three circumference passages, singular-versus-prefix matching, phrase boundaries between sections, apostrophes, and duplicate section rejection. The script and tests are included in the reference-data bundle.

Files and provenance

Lookup script · Checks · Contextual source compilation. The source record retains its own provenance and explains how contextual English differs from literal transliteration.

  https://jelliottdev.github.io/reference/lp1-10.html
- LP1-14
  https://jelliottdev.github.io/reference/lp1-14.html
- LP2-57
  https://jelliottdev.github.io/reference/lp2-57.html

  https://jelliottdev.github.io/reference/articles/transliteration.html
- rune indices and prime values
  https://jelliottdev.github.io/reference/articles/rune-values.html
- checksum guide
  https://jelliottdev.github.io/reference/articles/checksums.html
- circumference passages
  https://jelliottdev.github.io/reference/articles/circumference.html

  https://jelliottdev.github.io/scripts/reading_concordance.py

  https://jelliottdev.github.io/scripts/test_reading_concordance.py

Primality and divinity

Trace the words through The Loss of Divinity and the parable, then distinguish the mathematical definition from literary interpretation.

Primality and divinity meet in a specific claim in The Loss of Divinity: consumption, preservation, and adherence cause the loss of primality, and consequently divinity. The later parable describes divinity as something to find within. Reading the passages together gives the words a context; it does not turn them into a complete philosophical system or a cipher instruction.

Where the words occur

	Known-reading section	Contextual word position	What occurs there

	The Loss of Divinity
LP1-10–13	4	DIVINITY in the section heading.

	The Loss of Divinity	15	The opening statement introduces behaviors that cause its loss.

	The Loss of Divinity	152 and 156	PRIMALITY followed by DIVINITY in the concluding explanation of those behaviors.

	Parable
LP2-57	17	DIVINITY is described as within, between shedding circumferences and emerging.


The current compilation therefore contains one exact occurrence of PRIMALITY and four of DIVINITY, including the heading. These are positions in contextual English, counted from one at the start of each section. They are not rune positions, and a section spanning LP1-10–13 does not place each occurrence on all four pages.

What the passage actually argues

The sequence matters. Consumption is linked to perceived scarcity and fear of future inability to obtain what is needed. Preservation is linked to fear of being unable to regain what is lost. Adherence is linked to wanting to belong and be right. The text treats both dogma and reason as things that can be followed for that last motive. Its argument concerns dependence on possession and approval, rather than simply listing disfavored objects or beliefs.

	Step in the text	Connection

	Consumption · preservation · adherence	Behaviors assigned to the circumference.

	Loss of primality	The stated consequence of those behaviors.

	Loss of divinity	Presented as following from that loss of primality.


This table follows the passage’s argument, not an experimentally established causal chain. The text does not define a measurable quantity called divinity. Nor does its advice reduce to giving up possessions: the same section advises accumulating wealth while avoiding attachment to it. That distinction makes autonomy or freedom from dependence a plausible reading of what is being lost.

What primality means mathematically

An integer is prime when it is greater than one and has exactly two positive divisors: one and itself. For example, 13 has only 1 and 13; 15 also has 3 and 5, so 15 is composite. One is neither prime nor composite. “Indivisible” is a useful shorthand only if it means that there is no factorization into two integers both greater than one.

Gematria Primus assigns the first 29 primes to its 29 runes. Every individual rune value is therefore prime by construction. That does not make a word total prime: the F and U values, 2 and 3, sum to 5, while U and TH, 3 and 5, sum to 8. A property of each term need not survive addition.

There is thus a real mathematical context for the manuscript’s choice of vocabulary. But the statement about losing primality does not identify a number, a sum, or an operation. Moving from its wording to a calculation requires a further proposal. The prime-sum guide shows why the text layer, rune values, and boundaries all matter.

A mathematical metaphor, or something more?

One possible interpretation is that primality suggests an identity that cannot be factored into the possessions, affiliations, and descriptions attached to it. This can be compared with the first koan, where successive descriptions fail to answer who the student is. It is an analogy: people are not integers, and the manuscript does not explicitly equate a possession or affiliation with a factor.

A broader reading treats primality as an original or undivided condition, without requiring a literal arithmetic operation. The known passage does not settle between these interpretations. A useful comparison should explain the actual wording and its neighboring sentences, rather than relying on the word “prime” alone.

Likewise, “divinity within” permits an interpretation involving inward discovery, but does not identify a deity, religious school, or historical source. A proposed outside influence needs a specific textual or visual comparison. See outside works and attribution for the stronger and weaker kinds of connection already documented.

The Blake comparison examines a specific passage about inward deities and explains how its account differs from the manuscript’s parable.

How the parable changes the emphasis

[Image: LP2-57, containing the parable and its insect-like illustration]
LP2-57: the parable places inward divinity beside shedding and emergence. Open the reader for the complete image.

The earlier section describes a loss. The parable describes a movement: shed circumferences, find divinity within, and emerge. This gives the shared vocabulary a different role. Divinity is not only something the text says can be lost; it is also something its concluding parable asks the reader to discover.

The instar image supplies the biological comparison, while the circumference article follows the identity language through the second koan. Together these links let a reader examine the recurring terms without assuming that every drawing or sentence encodes the same operation.

Check the occurrences and arithmetic separately

Extract the reference-data ZIP and run these commands from its folder with Python 3. The concordance guide explains the matching and word-position rules.

python scripts/reading_concordance.py primality --context 18
python scripts/reading_concordance.py divinity --context 8
python scripts/reproduce_prime_sums.py

The first two commands locate vocabulary in the nine contextual sections. The third reproduces the separately documented sums using decoded rune sequences. A contextual word count is not an input to that sum calculation. Keeping the checks separate prevents expanded English spellings from silently changing the arithmetic.

Sources and further reading

The occurrence table and close reading use the known-reading compilation, especially The Loss of Divinity and LP2-57. The mathematical examples use the published rune values. Interpretations above are editorial comparisons, not additional decoded content. For actual numerical results, continue with prime sums, emirps, and spelling and prime sums.

Article: https://jelliottdev.github.io/reference/articles/primality-and-divinity.html

Rubrication: red lettering, numbers, and boundaries

Compare different uses of red in the manuscript and record color, text, and proposed cipher boundaries separately.

Rubrication is the use of red or otherwise distinguished lettering to help organize a manuscript. In Liber Primus, red appears in headings, larger opening marks, punctuation-like clusters, and decimal numbers. Those uses need to be recorded separately: a red number in a panel is not the same kind of feature as a red heading.

What does the term mean?

The Getty’s manuscript terminology entry includes headings, initials, titles, and other distinguished text used to guide readers through a page. Its Vidal Mayor lesson shows a red heading introducing a book within a larger work. This historical terminology helps describe a visual practice; it does not date Liber Primus or identify its maker.

A heading is identified by its position and function, while red lettering describes its appearance. A decoded title may establish a heading’s meaning. Color alone does not. For an unsolved passage, report the visible color and rune sequence before assigning a title.

The warning’s red closing phrase
Red lettering is not confined to headings. On LP1-01, it begins partway through the penultimate text row and continues on the last row, followed by a red cluster. The known reading joins the split word across those rows to give FOR ALL IS SACRED.
[Image: LP1-01 closing rows: black text changes to red partway through a row, with red writing continuing below.]
Original-image detail, rectangle [580, 2160, 1220, 400]. Complete page · Original JPEG.
The placement visually distinguishes the conclusion, but a description of color is not proof that the phrase needs a different cipher. The complete warning reproduction uses its documented Atbash reading. For the relation between the warning’s invitation to test and its demand to preserve the book, see questioning a book while preserving it.
Three different uses of red


[Image: LP2-15 preview showing a red rune heading and the red decimal entry 3299 among black numbers]
LP2-15: red runes above the panel; 3299 is the panel’s only red entry.

[Image: LP2-36 preview with a small red decimal 1 beside the start of a text block]
LP2-36: a red decimal 1 at the left of a text block.

[Image: LP2-57 preview with a red opening heading, a large angular red mark, and red dotted marks]
LP2-57: red opening text, an enlarged angular mark, and red dot clusters.


These previews are cropped. Open the reader to inspect each complete original. They illustrate different roles for color, not an exhaustive inventory of every red mark in the book.

LP2-15 is especially useful because the rune heading and number panel occur on the same page. The panel guide records all sixteen numbers and the heading. The red 3299 is an observable distinction; interpreting it as a key, ordinal, or instruction requires an additional rule. Likewise, a transliterated red rune group is not automatically decoded English.

LP2-57 provides a known-reading comparison. Its opening is read as PARABLE in the documented direct reading. That interpretation is supported by the recorded reading, not inferred from red alone. The prime-sum guide separately distinguishes the heading from three body segments and explains how including it changes the total.

For a closer comparison of one feature type, see the red closing clusters on LP2-22, LP2-32, and LP2-55. The enlarged original-image regions keep their color and orientation intact.

Red 1 and 2 across LP1-10–11
Red decimal labels also appear in the known readings. A red 1 introduces the lower passage on LP1-10; a red 2 opens LP1-11. The list crosses the page boundary.
[Image: LP1-10: a red 1 begins the numbered passage near the bottom of the text panel.]
LP1-10: first numbered error.
[Image: LP1-11: a red 2 begins the opening row, continuing the preceding page’s list.]
LP1-11: second numbered error.
The known reading identifies these as the two errors discussed under consumption: perceived insufficiency, then the belief that present resources came by luck and cannot be obtained again. This gives the numbering an established textual context. It is different from assigning a function to a red mark on an unsolved page using its color alone.
The page-by-page argument map follows the continuation into preservation and adherence. The red 1–5 labels on LP2-36–38 offer a separate, unsolved comparison; the known LP1 list does not establish what those later numbered blocks mean.
Can color mark a cipher boundary?

It can motivate a boundary hypothesis. A red heading followed by black body text gives a visible division worth checking. But several possibilities remain: the heading and body might share one transformation, use different transformations, or treat the heading as unencrypted. The image does not choose among them.

For a repeating-key proposal, even “skip the heading” is incomplete. Does the skipped heading consume key positions? Does the key restart at the next block or continue across it? The interruptions guide explains why the same visible boundary can lead to different outputs under different advancement rules.

The same issue affects measurements. The published whole-page IoC baseline includes archived rune headings. A body-only measurement would be a different input, not a corrected version of the baseline. Specify which rune positions were removed so another researcher can reproduce the comparison.

How to document a red feature


Identify the release and page, then open the original JPEG from its download record. Keep the image checksum with the observation.

Describe the feature’s location and type: heading, individual rune, number, dot cluster, or drawing. Do not merge unlike features into one “red text” stream without saying so.

Record the exact glyph sequence or decimal digits and its boundaries. If a crop is used, retain the full-image coordinates; the image-region guide explains that workflow.

Keep visible appearance separate from interpretation. “3299 is red” and “3299 selects a prime” are different claims.

For an extraction by pixel color, publish the thresholds, treatment of mixed edge pixels, and resulting mask. Check the mask against the original before treating it as a transcription.


A plain rune text file need not preserve color or layout. Do not assume that a punctuation character in an archive identifies a red mark. Compare the transcription conventions and original image, especially when proposing to extract only red material.

Sources and related subjects

Terminology: the Getty sources linked above. Examples: original page records for LP2-15, LP2-36, and LP2-57, with the LP2-15 observations and LP2-57 known reading already recorded in this wiki. Continue with dots and punctuation, the cuneiform-like page group, or the illustrated page index.

Color can also help locate writing outside the main text block. On LP1-04, the small red instruction beneath the main passage is easily lost at thumbnail size. The enlarged original-image detail keeps that line visible alongside its known reading.

Urizen: measurement and limits in Blake

Who the figure is, why he enters the cover discussion, and how to distinguish an artistic comparison from a cipher claim.

Urizen is a recurring character in William Blake’s poetry and designs. He matters to the cover discussion because the figure in The Ancient of Days is commonly identified with him. Recognizing a figure, understanding its role in Blake, and explaining its selection for a puzzle are separate questions.

[Image: Lower central panel of the preserved cover, with two golden compass legs extending upward from a hand]
Lower central panel, shown as a cropped view of the preserved cover. The compass legs extend upward in the collage. Compare the hand and rays around it with the complete frontispiece before interpreting this orientation. Open the complete original JPEG.

Who is Urizen?

The Blake Archive’s “Urizen, Bound and Unbound” discusses him as a character created by Blake, whose appearances vary across works. Its reading connects him with making laws and imposing limits. In the Europe frontispiece, his compasses support an interpretation of creation through measurement and boundaries.

The same essay contrasts that image with appearances in The First Book of Urizen, where bodily restriction and objects such as tablets and a book change the emphasis. It also notes uncertainty in identifying some other figures as Urizen. A bearded figure or a bent posture alone is therefore insufficient to identify every instance.

Why he enters the cover discussion

The lower compasses panel guide follows the published identification of the cover fragment and links the complete museum composition. That museum record qualifies the figure’s identity as “probably Urizen.” The Archive essay uses the name directly. Preserve each source’s wording rather than making them sound equally definite.

The cover isolates a fragment and changes its orientation. It does not display the full narrative setting of Blake’s work. Before interpreting a hand, instrument or ray of light, compare the complete preserved cover with the source composition. The adjacent Newton fragment provides a second depiction of measurement, but a repeated instrument is not a numerical extraction rule.

A comparison with circumference

Blake’s language of limits makes a comparison with circumference in Liber Primus worth articulating. The comparison should begin with the actual uses: the manuscript links circumference with the inner voice, dependence, and shedding. The Archive’s interpretation concerns a character’s role in Blake’s works. These are related subjects for reading, not interchangeable definitions.

	Question	Evidence needed

	Is the cover fragment from this composition?	Corresponding visual details, with crop, rotation and reflection recorded.

	How is Urizen interpreted in Blake?	A specified work and passage or image, with the interpretation attributed.

	Did the puzzle authors intend this connection?	Evidence beyond a compatible theme or an identified borrowed image.

	Does the name supply a working key?	A defined input, encoding, transformation and independently checkable result.


Continue reading

The Blake Archive essay, published 31 January 2018, supplies the character background above and illustrated comparisons across works. It is a discussion of Blake, not a source identifying the puzzle’s intentions. For the separate verbal parallel in the Welcome, see William Blake and Liber Primus. For the status of other proposed connections, use referenced works and possible influences.

Alphanumeric grids on LP2-49–51

Three plant-bordered sheets, 256 two-character entries, and a reproducible count that preserves case and leading zeroes.

LP2-49–51 contain rectangular arrays of two-character entries made from decimal digits and Latin letters. They are easy to recognize by the tall, curling plant borders on both sides. These arrays are different from the numerical magic squares: an arrangement in rows and columns does not by itself establish an arithmetic rule.

Where the grids appear


[Image: LP2-49: three runic rows above an alphanumeric grid, between plant borders.]
LP2-49: runes above the grid.

[Image: LP2-50: thirteen grid rows between plant borders.]
LP2-50: grid only.

[Image: LP2-51: nine grid rows followed by four runic rows.]
LP2-51: runes below the grid.


The first sheet has three runic rows above its grid, ending in a small red dotted cluster. The middle sheet has no runic rows. The third has four runic rows below the grid. The borders share curling stems, drooping leaves, root-like branches, and groups of filled dots. Compare the originals before treating the ornaments as identical copies.

The surrounding runic pages retain the paired borders: LP2-48 precedes the grids and LP2-52 follows them, each with twelve runic rows. Compare those layouts when deciding the bounds of an analysis.
What can be counted directly

	Page	Grid rows	Entries per row	Entries	Runes outside the grid
	LP2-49	10	8	80	66
	LP2-50	13	8	104	0
	LP2-51	9	8	72	92

Together, the archived grids contain (10 + 13 + 9) × 8 = 256 entries. Each entry contains two characters. The count 256 is therefore a count of entries, not runes, bytes, or distinct values. Calling these bytes would require an explicit decoding rule and a check of its outputs.

Repeated entries and distinct tokens

Counting exact two-character strings across all three archived grids gives 161 distinct tokens among the 256 entries. Of these, 92 occur once and 69 occur more than once. “Distinct tokens” counts different spellings; “entries” counts positions, including repetitions.

	Most frequent token	Occurrences
	0s	4
	1D	4
	1K	4
	2O	4
	2r	4
	3C	4

No token occurs more than four times in this transcription. For a concrete comparison, 0s occurs at LP2-49 row 5, column 5, and at LP2-50 row 5, column 5; row 6, column 4; and row 12, column 4. Grid row numbers exclude the runic text above or below the arrays.

Case must remain part of the comparison: 0X and 0x each occur three times, but they are separate tokens here. Repetition alone does not establish whether an entry represents a letter, a coordinate, a number, or something else. This inventory describes the archived data before choosing such an interpretation.

Reproduce the inventory

The JSON export includes an inventory with frequencies and sequence positions for every distinct token. Regenerating it with the export script recomputes those counts from the page records. This independent short calculation checks the headline counts from the exported entries:

import json
from collections import Counter
from pathlib import Path

data = json.loads(
    Path("exports/alphanumeric-grids.json").read_text(encoding="utf-8")
)
counts = Counter(row["token"] for row in data["records"])
print("entries", sum(counts.values()))
print("distinct", len(counts))
print("singletons", sum(n == 1 for n in counts.values()))
print("repeated tokens", sum(n > 1 for n in counts.values()))
print("maximum frequency", max(counts.values()))

Expected output: entries 256, distinct 161, singletons 92, repeated tokens 69, and maximum frequency 4. Sequence positions in the inventory point back to the coordinate-bearing records; they are not an additional decoding step.

Preserve the spelling of each entry

The first grid row on LP2-49 is 3N 3p 2l 36 1b 3v 26 33. Uppercase and lowercase letters both matter to the record: 0X and 0x, for example, appear as separate entries in its third row. Keep leading zeroes, too. Converting the entries to ordinary integers or uppercasing them would change the data before a hypothesis has been tested.

Some glyphs are easy to confuse, especially zero and uppercase O, or lowercase l and uppercase I. The stored transcription is a source you can reproduce, not a substitute for checking an ambiguous glyph against the original image. A proposed correction should identify its page, row, column, and image evidence. See the transcription guide for the distinction between an image and its text representation.

What an encoding proposal needs to specify

Reading these entries as positional numbers is a testable proposal. It needs an ordered alphabet, a base, an explanation of letter case, and a reading order across rows and pages. Names such as “base 60” or “base 62” alone do not provide that specification. Different symbol orders assign different values to the same entry.

For an alphabet of length b, a two-character entry xy would have value b × index(x) + index(y), using zero-based indices. That equation describes the proposed conversion; it does not show that the manuscript intended it. Keep the surrounding runes and artwork available as context, and distinguish a valid conversion from a demonstrated decipherment.

Reproduce the grid dimensions

Run this Python snippet from the repository root. It reads the archived page records, selects rows consisting entirely of hyphen-separated two-character alphanumeric entries, and checks that every selected row has eight entries. It does not choose a numeral base or change character case.

import json
import re
from pathlib import Path

total = 0
for number in (49, 50, 51):
    page_id = f"lp2-{number}"
    page = json.loads(
        Path(f"data/pages/{page_id}.json").read_text(encoding="utf-8")
    )
    rows = [
        line.removesuffix("/").split("-")
        for line in page["raw"].splitlines()
        if re.fullmatch(r"[0-9A-Za-z]{2}(?:-[0-9A-Za-z]{2})+/?", line)
    ]
    assert rows and all(len(row) == 8 for row in rows)
    count = sum(map(len, rows))
    total += count
    print(page_id, len(rows), 8, count)
print("total", total)

Expected output:

lp2-49 10 8 80
lp2-50 13 8 104
lp2-51 9 8 72
total 256

This check reproduces the dimensions of the stored transcription. It does not independently verify every glyph or prove that a particular traversal is intended. If you alter the transcription format, revisit the row-selection expression rather than assuming an unchanged count means an unchanged grid.

Download entries with coordinates

Use the structured JSON export for scripts or the CSV export for a table. Each entry keeps its page, grid row, column, sequence position, and original two-character token. Rows and columns start at one; the surrounding runic rows are not included in the grid row numbers.

The sequence follows pages 49, 50, and 51, reading each grid left to right and top to bottom. This is a reproducible export order, not a demonstrated cipher traversal. The JSON also records source-file and transcription checksums. Neither export normalizes case or removes leading zeroes.

When importing the CSV into a spreadsheet, set the token column to Text. Automatic number conversion can turn 04 into 4. Use the JSON when you need strings preserved without spreadsheet import settings.

Regenerate either format using the export script:

python scripts/export_alphanumeric_grids.py --format json
python scripts/export_alphanumeric_grids.py --format csv

Both commands print to standard output. The script rejects malformed rows or changed page dimensions rather than silently publishing an incomplete grid. It checks the archived structure; visual verification of ambiguous glyphs remains a separate task.

Originals and data

The page records for LP2-49, LP2-50, and LP2-51 link the original JPEGs, pinned archive sources, and checksums. Their machine-readable records are 49 JSON, 50 JSON, and 51 JSON. Return to the illustrated index to compare other manuscript details.

Transcendentalism: the context around Emerson

What the movement means, how it relates to Self-Reliance, and what the documented book-cipher use does and does not establish.

Transcendentalism is part of Emerson’s historical context. It enters this wiki through Self-Reliance, an essay used in the archived 2014 opening book cipher. That documented use makes Emerson worth reading; it does not automatically make the later manuscript a statement of transcendentalist doctrine.

What the name refers to

American transcendentalism was a nineteenth-century movement involving literature, philosophy, religion, and politics, centered around Ralph Waldo Emerson. Henry David Thoreau and Margaret Fuller were among its other important figures. Its writers criticized unthinking conformity and sought a more immediate relation to experience, nature, and spiritual life.

The movement developed amid New England religious debates and engagement with European thought, including Romanticism and German philosophy. It was broader than a slogan about independence: its participants also pursued publishing, educational and communal experiments, and social criticism. This introduction follows the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy’s historical account, revised 12 September 2023.

Transcendental is not the same as transcendent

In the Kantian background discussed by that source, transcendental concerns conditions through which experience becomes possible. It does not simply mean transcendent, or beyond experience. Emerson’s use is not identical to Kant’s, and the American movement should not be reduced to one technical definition.

This distinction matters when reading a theory: a word resembling a philosophical term is not yet an identification of the argument behind it. State which author, work, and passage you mean before comparing it with a manuscript sentence.

What can be compared with Liber Primus?

	Question	Passages to read together

	How does belonging influence judgment?	Emerson’s discussion of conformity in Self-Reliance and The Loss of Divinity.

	What does it mean to trust or examine the self?	Emerson’s self-trust and the two koans, which question descriptions of identity and the inner voice.

	What should a reader do with an inherited claim?	The essay’s criticism of conformity and the manuscript’s warning to test knowledge.


These are questions for comparative reading. For example, self-trust and the promised end to self are not interchangeable phrases. Before claiming agreement, identify what “self” means in each passage and what the speaker asks the reader to do. The circumference guide follows the manuscript’s own vocabulary across its known readings.

What the historical connection establishes

The reproduced book cipher establishes a concrete use of an Emerson text in the earlier puzzle route. It does not establish that Thoreau or Fuller supplied a manuscript source, that a particular philosophical doctrine is endorsed, or that a transcendentalist work is a key to an unsolved page.

A proposed literary source needs a traceable passage and a comparison of wording and structure. A proposed cipher key needs an explicit selection rule and a reproducible transformation. Use works and influences to distinguish those evidence types, and documenting an experiment to record a computational test.

Sources, related references, and files
- Self-Reliance; reproduced book cipher
  https://jelliottdev.github.io/reference/articles/emerson-self-reliance.html
- Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy’s historical account
  https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/transcendentalism/
- The Loss of Divinity
  https://jelliottdev.github.io/reference/articles/reading-loss-of-divinity.html
- the two koans
  https://jelliottdev.github.io/reference/articles/koans.html
- warning to test knowledge
  https://jelliottdev.github.io/reference/articles/reading-warning.html
- circumference guide
  https://jelliottdev.github.io/reference/articles/circumference.html
- works and influences
  https://jelliottdev.github.io/reference/articles/works-and-influences.html
- documenting an experiment
  https://jelliottdev.github.io/reference/articles/reproducibility.html

Pilgrimage, selfhood, and the Welcome

Follow the Welcome across LP1-03–04: loss of certainty, inward travel, emergence, and the tension between ending and commanding the self.

The Welcome addresses its reader as a pilgrim. Across LP1-03 and LP1-04, the journey becomes an account of losing certainty, reshaping reality and turning inward. This guide follows that movement within the known reading. It does not identify a particular religious pilgrimage or an undisclosed destination.

Read the two pages together

[Image: LP1-03, the first page of the Welcome]
LP1-03 introduces the pilgrim and the losses expected along the journey.
[Image: LP1-04, continuation of the Welcome and its instruction]
LP1-04 continues the sentence, then turns to emergence and self-command. Open either preview for the complete image.

The page break is not the end of the argument. The first page ends with the literal labels AN-END-TO-SELF; the next begins by describing what the pilgrimage shapes. Use the complete Welcome for both literal page readings and the contextual English.

How the journey changes meaning

	Movement in the passage	What to notice

	Arrival and invitation	The reader has found a place, but is addressed as someone beginning a difficult journey.

	Losses along the way	Relief from struggle and suffering appears in the same list as the loss of innocence, illusions, certainty and reality.

	The page break	An end to self is followed by a claim that the journey shapes ourselves and our realities.

	Inward movement	Going within is presented as the route to arriving outside and emerging.

	Closing instruction	The reader is addressed as an independent being and intelligence, then told to command the self.


The list of losses prevents a simple reading in which the journey only removes unpleasant experiences. It also removes things on which a person might rely when understanding the world. The following page describes formation as well as loss. Read together, these moves support an interpretation of pilgrimage as a transformation in how the self understands itself and reality.

Ending the self and commanding it

The Welcome does not finish at the claim about an end to self. It later addresses the reader as a being and a law unto themselves, affirms intelligence and life, and ends with self-command. Those statements should be read alongside the earlier loss, rather than silently dropping either side.

One interpretation distinguishes an identity that can be relinquished from the capacity to act or direct oneself. The text does not define two technical kinds of self, however. That distinction is a way to read the tension, not another sentence recovered from the runes. Compare the second koan’s inner voice, where a thought about the absence of a voice becomes an example of that voice.

Why the instar belongs here

The instar comparison links inward travel with emergence. An instar is a stage between molts; the guide explains how a stage differs from shedding and from the discarded covering. The Welcome uses this biological setting as an analogy, without specifying a species or developmental timetable.

The final parable returns to the instar, inward divinity and emergence, adding the shedding of circumferences. This repeated language connects the passages. It does not by itself settle the identity of the pictured insect or prescribe a cipher operation.

Check the reading before interpreting it

python scripts/reproduce_reading.py welcome
python scripts/reproduce_reading.py welcome --trace

Run these from the extracted reference-data bundle or repository with Python 3. The recorded Vigenère transformation continues across the two pages, with specified interruptions. The method section gives the key and exact counting rule. The trace exposes the transformations; it does not adjudicate a philosophical interpretation.

Preserve literal spellings and line wraps for arithmetic. For example, the word rendered contextually as pilgrimage is split across a line boundary on LP1-04. Contextual English helps reading, while literal labels and runes supply the inputs for sequence comparisons.

Sources and connected passages

This is an editorial close reading of the compiled known readings, checked against the two literal page exports. For an external textual comparison in the Welcome’s closing passage, see Blake and the statement about life being holy. That verbal parallel does not establish the source of the entire journey narrative. Continue with the philosophical reading route and circumference and identity.

Blake prints: plates, impressions, and copies

Understand relief etching and distinguish a composition, an individual print, and the digital image used for a cover comparison.

The cover studies refer to a design, a print, a copy, and a digital reproduction. These are different objects. Understanding the distinction helps explain why identifying a Blake composition does not automatically identify the image used in the compasses collage.

What is relief etching?

In Blake’s method, an acid-resistant drawing protected parts of a copper plate while exposed areas were etched lower. The remaining raised design could be inked and printed. Text and images could occupy the same plate; lettering was written backward so that the impression read in the intended direction. Prints could then receive further colouring and pen work. This summary follows Joseph Viscomi’s account of illuminated printing.

[Image: Schematic cross-section: ink sits on two raised areas of a plate; a print receives marks at the corresponding contact areas.]
A simplified relief-printing principle, not a reconstruction of a particular Blake plate. Heights and spacing are schematic. Open full size · Download SVG.

Blake called the process illuminated printing and its products illuminated books. Here “illuminated” names his way of making the work; it does not mean that the book is a medieval handwritten manuscript. Viscomi also distinguishes the history of the technique from later explanations of Blake’s motives for inventing it.

Which object are you comparing?

Design or composition
The arrangement of figures and other visual elements. Recognizing the hand and compasses concerns the design.
Printing plate or matrix
The physical surface from which an image is printed. It is not the paper image or a JPEG.
Impression
A particular print taken from that surface. Separate impressions can preserve the same design while differing in ink and finishing.
Copy of a book
A particular example of the book, identified by the catalogue. “Copy A” in the Europe record is not a claim about the puzzle image’s source.
Digital reproduction
A photograph or scan of an object. Its crop, resolution and colour appearance introduce another layer into a comparison.

Why the same design can look different

The Blake Archive describes variations caused by colour printing and subsequent finishing. Its 2012 publication announcement also explains that most of Blake’s large colour prints appear to have used a different kind of matrix from his relief-etched book plates. Do not assume that Newton, Nebuchadnezzar, and the Europe frontispiece were all made by one identical process.

For the cover, first compare the arrangement of details. Then ask whether a specific impression shares distinctive marks or colour placement. Finally compare the digital reproduction for matching crop and image defects. Record any rotation or reflection separately. A colour difference alone cannot decide whether the source was another impression or an altered reproduction.

Keep a useful comparison record

Save the collection identifier and source URL, the named copy or impression, and the exact region being compared. Separate observations from adjustments you made to align the images. The image-region guide explains pixel coordinates; the works index explains how to state the resulting claim. No printmaking term by itself supplies a cipher key.

Rune matches at a distance: lag coincidences

Compare runes at fixed distances, reproduce exact pair counts, and distinguish descriptive peaks from evidence of a period.

A lag is a distance between positions in a sequence. At lag 2, compare each rune with the rune two places later. Counting equal pairs gives an order-dependent description of the text: rearranging the same symbols can change the result, even when whole-page IoC stays unchanged.

A five-symbol example

For the teaching sequence ABABA, lag 2 makes three comparisons:

Position:   0  1  2  3  4
Sequence:   A  B  A  B  A

Compare 0 with 2: A = A
Compare 1 with 3: B = B
Compare 2 with 4: A = A

Matches: 3 out of 3

There is no comparison from the final A back to the beginning. This tool does not wrap around. Its complete result for the example is:

	Lag	Equal pairs	Pairs compared	Rate
	1	0	4	0
	2	3	3	1
	3	0	2	0
	4	1	1	1

The rate at lag 4 is also 1, but rests on just one pair. Always keep the denominator beside the rate. A large value supported by very few comparisons is not equivalent to a persistent pattern across many positions.

Reproduce the manuscript calculation

Extract the reference-data bundle with its folders intact. Python 3 and its standard library are sufficient:

python scripts/rune_lag_matches.py lp2-31 --max-lag 4
python scripts/rune_lag_matches.py lp2-31 --max-lag 20 --output lp2-31-lags.json
python scripts/test_rune_lag_matches.py

The first command reports 0/268, 9/267, 5/266, and 10/265 for lags 1–4. The JSON also gives reduced fractions and decimal rates. These are descriptive counts from the archived 269-rune stream, not a newly established key period or solution.

The default maximum lag is 20; explicitly choose a smaller value for a shorter stream. Valid lags run from 1 to one less than the rune count. The output option refuses to overwrite an existing file. The script uses rune_ngrams.py from the same bundle to identify runes; keep that helper beside it.

Inspect all twenty distances

[Image: Bar chart of equality rates at lags one through twenty on LP2-31, with a dashed count-preserving shuffle expectation. The reference line is not a significance threshold.]
All lags 1–20 under the same archived-rune rule. The number of compared pairs decreases from 268 to 249. Open full size · Download chart (SVG).

Download the CSV table for a spreadsheet, or the JSON report for the complete counting rule and shuffle model. Each CSV row retains its numerator, denominator, input path and source hash. The dashed line is an expected rate under the stated model, not a cutoff for an interesting result.

To reproduce the chart, use the extracted reference-data bundle and install matplotlib in your Python environment, then run:

python scripts/plot_rune_lags.py --output my-lag-chart.svg

The plotting script reads the included JSON; it does not recalculate or alter the rune stream. The counting script remains standard-library only. Keep the plotting-library version with shared figures; visual formatting can vary between versions. Existing output files are not overwritten.

What exactly is counted?

The script retains archived runes in order, including headings, and removes non-runes. Pairs may therefore cross word, line, and paragraph breaks, but never page boundaries. It performs no spelling conversion, correction, decoding, or interruption skipping. The report records the input file, its SHA-256, the alphabet, and its hash.

For a stream of length n and a lag d, the denominator is n − d. The numerator counts indices i = 0, …, n − d − 1 for which x[i] = x[i+d]. These are forward pairs counted once. They are different from the all-position ordered pairs in the ordinary IoC formula.

What would a shuffled stream give?

Under a uniform random rearrangement preserving the symbol counts, any two distinct positions have expected equality rate Σ c(c−1) / [n(n−1)]. Each fixed-lag pair uses two distinct positions, so averaging their equality indicators gives that same expectation. This derives an expected rate, not a distribution of possible peaks.

The report includes this fraction as shuffle_expected_rate_fraction. It is not a p-value, a confidence interval, or a threshold for a meaningful result. Pairs can overlap, and results at different lags share the same input. If you select the largest result after scanning many lags, a chance comparison must repeat that selection procedure. See null models and selection.

How all distances add up to IoC

Every pair of distinct positions has exactly one positive distance. If you calculate all lags from 1 through n − 1, you count every forward pair once. Consequently:

Matching forward pairs
Σ c(c−1) / 2
All forward pairs
n(n−1) / 2
Ratio of these totals
Whole-page IoC

Here c is each symbol’s frequency. Both totals are half the ordered-pair totals used in the IoC formula, so their ratio is unchanged. This is an identity for the observed stream, not just an average expected from shuffling.

In the ABABA example, combine the counts: (0 + 3 + 0 + 1) / (4 + 3 + 2 + 1) = 4/10. The same stream has three As and two Bs, giving IoC (3×2 + 2×1) / (5×4) = 8/20. Both equal 2/5.

Do not average the four rates equally. That would give (0 + 1 + 0 + 1) / 4 = 1/2, because it assigns a one-pair lag the same weight as a four-pair lag. Weight each rate by its number of comparisons, or simply divide the summed numerators by the summed denominators.

The LP2-31 chart above includes only lags 1–20, so its pooled rate need not equal whole-page IoC. For the identity, all 268 distances are required. Lag counts reveal how matching pairs are distributed over distances; their full total supplies no independent evidence beyond the same frequency counts.

What the result cannot decide

An elevated lag can motivate a more specific test; it does not identify a cipher or key length by itself. Changing the heading policy, page boundaries, or skipped positions changes the sequence being measured. Record those choices before comparing reports.

Renaming symbols consistently leaves equality unchanged. Reversing the whole stream also preserves the count at each lag, because it pairs the same positions in the opposite direction. This statistic therefore cannot choose between a stream and its reversal. For local repeated patterns and their source positions, use the n-gram tool; for the broader principle, read what operations preserve.

Files and checks

Calculation script · Checks. Tests also check the all-lag identity on every three-symbol sequence of lengths 2–6. They cover the hand example, valid lag bounds, symbol renaming, reversal, and the expected rate averaged over all six distinct arrangements of AABB. The archived-page check verifies the 269-rune scope and its comparison denominators. These validate the stated calculation, not the original photographic transcription.

THE LOSS OF DIVINITY THE CIRCUMFERENCE PRACTICES THREE BEHAVIORS WHICH CAUSE THE LOSS OF DIVINITY CONSUMPTION WE CONSUME TOO MUCH BECAUSE WE BELIEVE THE FOLLOWING TWO ERRORS WITHIN THE DECEPTION 1 WE DO NOT HAVE ENOUGH, OR THERE IS NOT ENOUGH 2 WE HAVE WHAT WE HAVE NOW BY LUCK; AND WE WILL NOT BE STRONG ENOUGH LATER TO OBTAIN WHAT WE NEED MOST THINGS ARE NOT WORTH CONSUMING PRESERVATION WE PRESERVE THINGS BECAUSE WE BELIEVE WE ARE WEAK IF WE LOSE THEM WE WILL NOT BE STRONG ENOUGH TO GAIN THEM AGAIN THIS IS THE DECEPTION MOST THINGS ARE NOT WORTH PRESERVING ADHERENCE WE FOLLOW DOGMA SO THAT WE CAN BELONG AND BE RIGHT; OR WE FOLLOW REASON SO WE CAN BELONG AND BE RIGHT THERE IS NOTHING TO BE RIGHT ABOUT; TO BELONG IS DEATH IT IS THE BEHAVIORS OF CONSUMPTION, PRESERVATION AND ADHERENCE THAT HAVE US LOSE OUR PRIMALITY, AND THUS OUR DIVINITY SOME WISDOM AMASS GREAT WEALTH NEVER BECOME ATTACHED TO WHAT YOU OWN BE PREPARED TO DESTROY ALL THAT YOU OWN AN INSTRUCTION PROGRAM YOUR MIND PROGRAM REALITY

A Koan: second section: complete reading

Vigenère; LP1-14, LP1-15. Literal pages, contextual text, and exact reproduction.

This known section covers LP1-14 · LP1-15, in that order. The literal readings below preserve individual page boundaries. The contextual English at the end describes the whole section.
For the meaning and relationship of the dialogues, read The two koans: identity and the inner voice.
Method and reproduction
Vigenère: worked explanation. The recorded transformation is p = (c − key[j mod key length]) mod 29, using zero-based positions in the 29-rune alphabet.
Key indices: 0, 10, 4, 0, 1, 19, 0, 18, 4, 18, 9, 0, 18.
Start at sequence position 0. Carry the sequence across the listed page boundaries. Non-rune characters do not consume key positions.
Copy these zero-based rune ordinals without advancing the sequence: 49, 58. See interruptions and counting conventions; these recorded positions are not a universal rule for other pages.
python scripts/reproduce_reading.py second-koan
python scripts/reproduce_reading.py second-koan --trace

An End: the hash reference: complete reading

Prime-minus-one; LP2-56. Literal pages, contextual text, and exact reproduction.

This known section covers LP2-56, in that order. The literal readings below preserve individual page boundaries. The contextual English at the end describes the whole section.
Method and reproduction
Prime-minus-one: worked explanation. The recorded transformation is p = (c − (prime[j] − 1)) mod 29, using zero-based positions in the 29-rune alphabet.
Start at sequence position 0. Reset the sequence at the page boundary. Non-rune characters do not consume key positions.
Copy these zero-based rune ordinals without advancing the sequence: 56. See interruptions and counting conventions; these recorded positions are not a universal rule for other pages.
python scripts/reproduce_reading.py lp2-56
python scripts/reproduce_reading.py lp2-56 --trace
Run with Python 3 from the extracted reference-data bundle or a full repository checkout. The script checks its result against the shipped literal controls before printing. It uses no network or AI requests. Read the script · Exact parameters and provenance.
